It has been thought desirable to complete, with as little delay as possible, this important link in the chain of Danish railways, as it will, in conjunction with the North of Europe Steam Navigation Company, at once establish a communication with the Baltic by the shortest possible transit. Passengers will be able to go from London and the principal ports of England to Tonning and Flcnsburg (on the Baltic) in 30 to to 34 hours ; in Copenhagen in 48 hours ; and Hamburg to 36 hours, including the overland journey by railway. Some idea of the enormous trade of these countries may be formed from the fact that upwards of 14,000 vessels pass the Sound annually. Their cargoes, independently of those that pass in ballast, may be roughly estimated at 1,500,000 tons. The Sound dues levied thereupon, at a toll varying from one to one-aud-a-quarter per cent, produce a revenue of more than 150,000/. ; we may, therefore, safely calculate the value of the same at 15,000,000/. sterling. For the purpose of calculating the probable return on the outlay in constructing the Railway, a careful estimate has been made of the amount

ami description of goods, both import and export , that may be expected to pass over the line, and he aggregate amount has been ascertained to be little less than 200,000 tons. The local traffic alone, as given in Government returns of tolls received on the ordinary road, amounts at the present time to 36,000/. a year ; and assuming the usual increase through the improved facilities, that is to say, doubling it, we have a gross annual return of 72,000/. ; so that, making the largest allowance for working expenses, this branch of income alone will suffice to pay an interest of 6 percent, on the entire capital. John Ericsson, the distinguished engineer, (son of a large, mining proprietor,) was born on the 31st of July 1808, in the province of Vermelund, Sweden He showed a surprising mechanical capacity when quite a child, and at the age of eleven years attracted the attention of the celebrated Count Platen, Viceroy of Norway, who procured his appointment as a cadet in a corps of engineers, and in 1816 he was made nivelleur on the grand ship Canal, between the Baltic and the North Sea. He entered the Swedish array in 1819, and by this step lost the favour of his potron. In the army he rose rapidly, and obtained his rank of captain from King Charles John, better known as Bernadette, one of þÿNapoleon ablest s marshals ; and, shortly after his promotion, was employed some time in the survey of Northern Sweden. Tu the meanwhile, he devoted much time to his favorite speculations in mechanics,

and projected the Flame Engine, one of the earliest of his þÿinventions intended to work independently of steam, by condensing flame. In 1826 he hoped to bring this into public England, he obtained permission to visit notice, but he where soon discovered that when the engine was worked by mineral fuel, it proved unsuccessful. In 1829 he competed for the purse offered by the Liverpool and Manchester railway for the best Locomotive, and produced an engine which attained the astonishing speed of fifty miles an hour, thus planning the first locomotive of high speed, the celebrated Novelty, Thus, his first tained within months of the first trial, engine a rate of atone mile in 59 seconds. In connection with it may be stated that Ericsson is the first this, man who ever built a tubular boiler with artificial draft. The steam fire engine also owes its origin to his inventive genius. Before leaving England he planned several such engines, which were used with great effect. He received a magnificent gold prize medal from the New York Meþÿchanic Institute s for this invention. Since Mr þÿEricsson residence s in the United States, he has been the author of many inventions which have made his name familiar to the public. It is well known that he introduced the screw propellor into practical use here. The English give him credit for having been chiefly instrumental in introducing the screw propellor. He can also claim the honor of having solved the problem of producing a ship of war with the whole of her machinery

below the water-line, having planned and superintended the construction of the machinery of the 1 nited States Steam Frigate Princeton þÿ admitted all over the world to be the most complete vessel of war in existence. His improvements in managing heavy naval ordnance furnishes another instance of his fertility of invention. In the American department of the great exhibition, he displayed an instrument for measuring distance at sea ; the hydrostatic gauge for measuring the volume of fluids under pressure, the reciprocating fluid meter, the alarm barometer, the pyrometer, the rotary fluid meter, and the sea lead, all of which he has given a brief explanation in a communication addressed to Prince Albert. For these instruments he received the prize medal of the exhibition. The invention, however, which has lately attracted most attention, is the Caloric engine, intended to supercede the use of steam . Captain Ericsson first brought this remarkable production before the scientific world in London, in 1833, when he constructed an engine of five horse power and exhibited it to a number of scientific gentlemen. But although it met with the approbation of the celebrated Faraday, Dr. Andrew Ure, l)r. Lardner and others, from that time to the present, Capt. Ericsson has pursued the subject and built a number of experimental engines, removing practical difficulties step by step, until it is presented complete to the world. In testimony of his many useful inventions, he has

received in several countries, prize medals, some of which are of great value. He is a Knight of the Order of Vasa, and a member of many scientific societies, and we also add with much satisfaction that lie has become a citizen of the l "nited States. þÿ N. Y. Illustrated News.

Popular Fallacies about tlie Tloou. The laborious researches of M. Arago respecting the supposed influence of the moon on the state of the weather, and on animal and vegetable bodies, have tended materially to clear up a subject on which there has long prevailed much prejudice and superstition. These researches were ably reported in two articles in the Monthly Chronicle, and from them we propose to lay some instructive and amusing particulars before our readers. The Influence of the Moon on the Weather forms the subject of the first article. From a very early period, meteorological phenomena were supposed to be connected with the lunar motions ; nor was this supposition unnatural, considering the obvious and undeniable, though at the same time mysterious, influence of the same planet on the tides. Originally, however, the moon and other heavenly bodies were regarded more as signs than causes, as far as atmospheric phenomena were concerned ; but in course of time these signs degenerated into a most absurd system of rules, having no real foundation in nature. The following, for example, is one of the axioms regarding the þÿmoon s influence : þÿ If the horns of the lunar crescent, on the third day after new moon, are sharply and clearly defined, the weather may be expected to be fair during the ensuing month. The absurdity of this is made apparent by the plain argumentation subjoined. þÿ The lunar crescent is produced by a peculiar relation of position which subsists between lie aspects of the moon presented to the sun and

the earth. If only'half the hemisphere which receives the þÿsun l s ight be presented towards the earth, the moon is exactly halved ; if a quarter of the hemisphere be turned to the earth, the moon is a crescent, and its age is then nearly four days. When its age is less than two days, therefore, less than an eight of its illuminated hemisphere is presented to our planet, and consequently it appears as a very thin crescent. It is evident that these effects, if seen through perfectly transparent space, could not alter with circumstances; and that, in the same position of the moon, with respect to the earth and sun, the crescent must be at all times equally sharp and distinct. But when the moon is viewed, as it is by us, through an atmosphere from thirty to forty miles high þÿ that atmosphere being liable to be more or less loaded with imperfectly transparent vapours þÿ it will be seen with more or less distinctness, according to the varying transparency of the medium through which it is viewed. The fact, therefore, of the crescent appearing distinct and well defined, or obscurely with the points of the horns blunted, is merely a consequence of our atmosphere being at one time more pure, clear, and transparent, than at þÿanother. Another axiom of lunar meteorology declares, that 1 if on the fourth day the moon project no shadow, we are to expect bad weather during the þÿmonth. In this instance, also, the moon simply serves as an instrument to determine the humidity of the air; for as the quan-

tity of light reflected from the moon must be always the same, its intensity on reaching our earth, or, in other words, its power to produce a shadow, must be determined by the amount of vapours in the atmosphere which it passes through. The pnqiosition, therefore, is identical with the last ; and only means, that when þÿ the atmosphere in the west, a little after sunset, on the fourth day of the moon, is loaded with humidity, the weather during the month will be þÿbad. These two propositions, accordingly, couched under such seemingly profound terms, signify no more than that we shall always have bad weather during any given month, if the atmosphere in the western horizon is vapoury for an hour or two, on a certain evening, towards, its beginning þÿ a proposition most superlatively lame, impotent, and inconclusive. The ingenious writer of these papers, after exhibiting the fallacy of such axioms as these, proceeds to examine the justice of the very common notion, that þÿ a change of weather accompanies a change of the þÿmoon. þÿ I lie long train of scientific reasoning which follows on this subject would occupy too much of our space, and we shall content ourselves, therefore, with stating the conclusion to which the writer arrives. þÿ From all that has been stated, it follows then, conclusively, that the popular notions concerning the influence of the lunar pit tses on the weather have no foundation in theory, and no correspondence with observed facts. That the moon, by her gravitation, exerts an attraction on our

atmosphere, cannot be doubted ; but its effects are either too small in amount to be appreciable in the actual state of meteorological instruments, or they are obliterated by other more powerful causes, from which they have not yet been þÿeliminated. Toe notion, therefore, that a change is to be looked for at full and new moon, venerable as that notion is from its antiquity and the universality of its acceptation, receives no countenance from the results of scientific inquiry. The supposed influence of the moon is not confined to the weather, (iardeners in some countries have an idea that the red moon kills the young shoots of plants. The red moon is that which is full between the middle of April and the close of May. Now, in charging such a moon with an injurious effect on plants, the accusers simply mistake a sign for a cause. Plants are killed frequently at that season as if by frost, though, on the nights when the death takes place, a thermometer in the open air may stand many degrees above the freezing-point. Observing this to be the case, gardeners can see no cause for the evil done to the plants but the lunar light, which they notice to be always keen and strong at the period. But, in reality, the state of the atmosphere is the true cause of the injury to the vegetables. On clear and unclouded nights, substances on the þÿearth surface s lose heat by radiation, while the sky is not in a state to restore to them any of their lost warmth. Ice is, in fact, produced in warm
climates, under such circumstances. But if the atmos-

3 T Giants: a t a s phere be clouded, these clouds, having the quality of radiating heat, restore the caloric radiated from substances on the surface of the earth. On cloudy nights, accordingly, when the moon is veiled, plants receive no injury by the radiation of their heat ; while, on cloudless nights, when the moon is vivid and unveiled, plants are injured. The moon falsely bears the blame, whereas, in reality, she is only a sign of that condition of the atmosphere which is justly chargeable with the injury. There is another equally erroneous aphorism respecting the influence of the moon on vegetables. Almost all European gardeners and agriculturists hold that vegetables, plants, and trees, which are expected to thrive, should be planted, grafted, and pruned, during the increase of the aioon. One supporter of this theory has thus attempted to prove its accordance with physical principles : þÿ During the day, the solar heat augments the quantity of sap which circulates in plants, by increasing the magnitude of the tubes through which the sap moves ; w hile the cold of the night produces theopposite effect, by contracting these tubes. Now, at the moment of sunset, if the moon be increasing, it will be above the horizon, and the warmth of its light would prolong the circulation of the sap ; but, during its decline, it w ill not rise for a considerable time after sunset, and the plants will be suddenly exposed to the unmitigated cold of the night, by which a sudden contraction of leaves and tubes will be produced, and the circula-

tion of the sap as suddenly þÿobstructed. This is the best reasoning which can be adduced by its supporters in favour of this doctrine, and, unfortunately for them, the whole can be very simply shewn to be based on error þÿ though no matter of moonshine. þÿ If we þÿadmit, says the writer in the Monthly Chronicle, þÿ the lunar rays to possess any sensible calorific power, this reasoning might be allowed, but it will have very little force when it is considered that the extreme change of temperature which can be produced by the lunar light doe8 not amount to the ten-thousandth part of a degree of the þÿthermometer! But, in truth, argumentation is not required to overturn this fallacy. It is enough that experiment decisively shews, that tto appreciable difference can be observed in the qualities of vegetables planted at different times in the lunar month. þÿ"Plinv s prescription of the full moon as the time for bean-sowlentils ng. and in the earth, excites a smile in M. Arami. þÿ of the new moon as the season of putting Truly" we have þÿneed, says he, þÿ of a robllst faith to þÿadmit without proot, that the moon, at the distance of 240 000 miles, shall in one position act advantageously on the vegetation of beans, and that, at the same distance, and in the opposite position, she shall be propitious to þÿlentils. which seem to be more properly attributable to other causes. The þÿsun rays s have, it is well known, a striking effect on the colour of many objects, but the moon's rays appear to possess but little of the same power. The white chloride of silver becomes a deep black when laid in the sun, while the þÿmoon s rays do not affect in the least. This, and other circumstances, lead us to doubt the þÿmoon p s ower in blackening the skin. M. Arago thinks it not improbable, that the radiation of utirestored heat from the skin may tend to darken its hue when exposed to the air on a clear cold night. Bivouacking by night in the open air soon deepens the tint of the human (ace. But here it is not the moon that acts, although the true cause will operate often when the moon is unveiled by clouds, as in the case of the vegetables already adverted to. A clear moonless night will have the same effect as a clear night with a visible moon. There is a prevailing notion amongst butchers, in some parts of the world, that the marrow found in the bones of animals varies in quantity according to the phase of the moon in which they were slaughtered. Experiments, instituted for the purpose, have proved this belief to be without foundation, and this is the only mode of refutation which the subject will admit of. The same answer may be given to the assertions, that shell-fish become larger during the increase than during the decline ol the moon, and that a healthy man gains 2 poundweights at the beginning of every lunar

month, which he looses ere its end. Experiment disproves both. Another common idea is, that putrefaction is forwarded by the light of the moon. This is another instance þÿ if the fact really be as stated þÿ of the substitution of the moon for the clear sky, which permits the inoon to lie visible. It is in clear nights that dew is deposited, and humidity lias a tendency to accelerate putrefaction. Passing over several minor instances, noticed by our authority, of supposed lunar influence, we come to that opinion which has given origin to the word lunatic, as applied to insane persons. The second Danish Chamber has rejected the state budget of 13,307,054 rix dollars, demanded by the government, and passed one granting 13, ()(>(», I7G rix dollars. The receipts are estimated at 13,795,198 rix dollars. Letters from Kiel correct the telegraphic account on the faith of which it has been asserted that the Danish Diet had approved the royal message on a third deliberation. On the contrary, the success of the present ministers appeared very problematical on the 15th, when the third deliberation was to commence. YY'e learn by electric telegraph from Copenhagen that in consequence of the rejection of the royal message the Chambers were dissolved on Tuesday last. New elections are appointed, those for the Folkething (Lower House) on the 27th of May, and those for the Landsthing (Upper House) on the 3rd June next. It is stated that the Ministers Bang and Simony have resigned. On the 18th ult., tiie question of the succession was brought to a division and lost, the majority of 97 to 45 not reaching the requisite proportion of threefourths ot the votes present. Eight members abstained from voting; only one member of the whole Rigsdag was absent. On the following day the Rigsdag was dissolved. The election for the Folkething is fixed for the 27th of May; the primary election to the Landsthing for

A T I \ the 13th of May, the secondary for the 3rd of June. The new Rigsdag will thus hardly come together before the middle of June, whilst the provisional powers with reference to the supplies extend only to the 31st ot May. It is rumoured that the Minister ot the Interior, Bang, the Minister of Education, Simony, and even the Minister The tice, Scheel, would retire. ot Jus- announcement of the dissolution in the Folkething produced a thundering "bravo" for the King and for the 45 minority. Letters from Copenhagen of the 22nd report a partial change in the Danish cabinet. The jurist Orsted, who, by his friendly amendment to the resolution of the Cabinet, moved in the late Diet, brought the Government more votes than it had before been able to obtain, is admitted into the Ministry. M. Bang remains, as well as M. Bluhme. M. Simony, Minister of Justice, it is said, retires.

YYre are gratified to observe that the British Government hasappointed a commission to attend the opening ot the New Y ork Exhibition on the 1st ot June next. This is a graceful and friendly act towards the American people which cannot be too much admired, and the moral effect of which will go tar to counteract any prejudice which may exist in the minds of our transatlantic cousins arising out of the " Stowe movement" in this country. The selection ot persons composing this commission is also made in the best possible taste. At the head of it stands the Earl ot Ellesmere, þÿ -a nobleman as much distinguished tor his fine taste as for his unbounded wealth and refined liberality. It the English peerage had been ransacked tor a person the most suitable to be placed at the head of a mission of love of this kind, þÿ a model nobleman, the one atrove all others whose virtues and talents the Americans were most likely to appreciate, þÿ no one could have been selected possessing higher qualification than the Earl of Ellesmere. He is not only a man of fine literary capacity and scientific skill, but lieis wedded to the interests of commerce in a manner more close than any other nobleman in the kingdom. With Lord Ellesmere have been associated five other gentlemen, all of them eminent in their respective spheres. 8ir Charles Lyell, the distinguished geoloessentially to the gist, and Mr. Dilke, success who contributed so of the Great London Exhibition, are men especially fitted, by their attainments and their

habits of observation, to represent the industrial interests of England on so interesting an occasion. Professor YYblson will personify agricultural science, as tar as it has hitherto been developed in this country; Mr. YVallis, a gentleman long before the public in connexion with textile fabrics, and with efforts to educate the artistic eye of operatives, is another happy selection ; while the celebrated tool manufacturer, Mr.YY hitworth, whose ingenuity as a mechanic as is a only surpas- sed by his excellence man, completes a batch of as able persons as ever left the shores of England on a scientific mission. To impart to the affair all the imprcssiveness of which it is susceptible, the commissioners will be conveyed across the Atlantic in steam frigates belonging to the Royal Navy, and their

stay will be sufficiently long to effect all the purposes which are to be derived from a friendly interchange of courtesies, and with giving and receiving every available information connected with the highest developments of productive skill, and the advancement of man. þÿ Ibid.

The French news continues to be almost wholly limited to objects of purely an administrative character. The reasons for the relinquishment of the scheme of the transatlantic packet station are now set forth officially. In one word, it was found to be too costly, ft would have required twenty-nine vessels, propelled by I7,(500-horse power, and as the subvention required from the state was quite disproportionate to the probable receipts, the plan was abandoned under the pretence that modern discoveries tended to the belief that a vast reduction in the consumption of fuel might be effected, and it would be better for France to wait until this was accomplished. The Government has suspended the concession of the service of the transatlantic lines, but has resolved to establish within a short time a line of communication with Brazil. The Empress has been so milch indisposed within these few days that she has not appeared in public. As crowned female sovereigns are not spoken of with so much reserve and delicacy as married women in humbler spheres, we are told in pretty plain language that "love's labour has been lost." The day on which this occurrence took place is specified, and thus the hopes raised from the alleged interesting situation of the Empress, of a future heir to the throne of France, are for the present, entirely at an end. The Empress was not present at the ball at the Tuileries on Monday, and the Emperor retired at a very early hour, leaving, however,

5000 guests to enjoy the pleasures of the dance until a later hour of the night. M. G uizot appeared in public, and presided at the anniversary meeting of the Society for the Encouragement of Elementary Schools. In a very eloquent speech he attempted to console his auditory for the loss of political liberty, by assuring them that the religious movement had never been greater. Religious liberty supplied the loss of political liberty, for which the French were not fitted. Religion is to save France from further evils, and faith is to do the good work of the Roman Catholic Church. An " infernal machine," completely mounted, has been discovered on board a vessel just arrived from Rio Janeiro at Havre. The information which led to the discovery proceeded from the French Minister at Rio, and a locksmith, who had been resident at Rio some years, and who was on board the vessel, was arrested, with his wife, and lodged in prison. The Danish Ministry has been changed in consequence of the recent vote on the law of succession. 0r>ted is the new President of the Council, and Bluhme has the foreign portfolio. þÿ Ibid.

The story of the unfortunate Dufavel, who was buried accidentally in a well, and remained in it for a long period, is not without a parallel in the history of mining transactions in France. In the department of the Indre, and parish of Fleure-la- Riviere, March 27, 1837, about half-past eight in the morning, Etienne Billard, a working-mason, descended a well 120 feet deep, for the purpose of examining it preparatory to some repairs. When he had reached the bottom, or nearly so, an extensive portion of the sides fell in upon him, and shut him out from the light of day; but, by a remarkable piece of good-fortune, the materials, in falling, formed a small arch of about three feet in diameter around his head. Had it not heen for this, he would have been either fatally hurt by the heavy stones of the masonry, or would have been suffocated immediately. Every other part of the well around his body was filled compactly with the fallen materials. The noise of the irruption was heard by some workmen near the spot, who immediately ran up to it. On listening certainty that he was yet alive, inspired intently, they heard the cries of Billard, the and the hope of delivering him. Sending off one of their number to alarm the neighbouring inhabitants and authorities, these workmen then lowered a lighted candle down the well, the danger of a further fall ot the sides deterring themselves from going down. The candle went down 100 feet, thus shewing that about twenty feet of the mass, or a consider-

able portion thereof, lay above the unfortunate Eillard. In reply to their call, he was heard distinctly to say, of the light. ' I am assured,' he moreover said, that he could not see anything ' that I am a lost man. But I suffer no pain, and I breathe freely.' No ordinary difficulty, it was obvious, stood in the way of relief in this case. For workmen to descend into the narrow deep well, and attempt to clear away the ruins, without some security task. The authorities of against a further fall of the the sides, was a dangerous district, as soon as they arrived, and saw the nature of the accident, sent off an express for the district-superintendent of roads and bridges, M Certain, lie was at some distance, and did not arrive till next day. In the meantime, one man, a slater, ventured to descend to the top of the fallen mass of stones and earth, which proved, as had been shewn by the candle, to be about 100 feet below the orifice. Urged by the indistinct cries for help which they heard from poor Billard, the men on the spot began to lift the stones forming the he sides well. When M. Certain arrived, descended of the without hesitation into the well, and put several questions to Billard respecting his situation. M. Certain judged it proper to continue the raising of the sides of the well, as the displacement of the lower part would render it most imprudent to go on otherwise. No side-boring could be executed with such speed as the whole well could be cleared. The soil, fortunately, was clayey and

firm. While this labour was going on day and night, with the utmost rapidity compatible with a proper degree of caution, friends and fellow-workmen of Billard descended occasionally to animate him with the cheering sound of kindly voices, and with the assurance that help was near. On the morning of the 2!)th, the governor and head-engineer of the department of the Indre with rived. M. Ferrand, inspector of works, was arthem, and descended into the well, lie gave his assent to the continuation of the operations going on, which some of the anxious friends of the prisoner were beginning to exclaim against, from their seeming slowness. In presence of the gentlemen mentioned, the labours were continued, and on the evening of the 29th, the well was clear to the upper part of the fallen mass. \\ itliout delay, the process of lifting them was begun ; but from the size of the stones, the work went on very tardily, through the difficulty of hoisting them to such a distance above. After tlicy had advanced a certain way, a new difficulty met them in the face. It was impossible to tell the exact state of the arch formed so miraculously over the head of the unfortunate man, or its degree of stability. It was necessary, therefore, to go on with the elevation of the stones with extreme care and delicacy, otherwise the unsettlement of any portion of the heavy masses above him might have caused his instantaneous death, either from a crush or suffocation. At ten o'clock in the evening of the 29th, the

workmen were calculated to be about six feet above the captive, who had now been shut out from the light since the morning of the 27th. It was impossible to send him food by a bore, as in the case of Dufavel, and he had therefore the pressure of hunger added to his misery. His voice was heard more clearly as the workmen went on, and they could now even tell the exact point where he was confined. But during the

3 ® 'ii © !t A 'f It 3> night of the 29th, his voice became a source of fear and alarm to the labourers above him. Billard's motionless condition, his want of food and air for so long a time, began to overthrow his moral courage, llis reason gave place to delirium, his hope to despair. The workmen heard him at one moment lamenting his fate, and piteously crying for food, and at the next moment they heard him abandoning himself to the most extravagant gaiety. Laughter heard in such a situation was a thing almost too deplorable and shocking for human ears to listen to. When consulted on the meaning of these symptoms on the part of Billard, M. Nabert, a surgeon, who had never quitted the spot since the time to of the accident, recommended the workmen hurry on their labours, as the man could probably survive but a few hours in this state. In consequence of this advice, a new direction was given to the work, and in place of passing down by the side of the spot where the poor man was supposed to be, the excavation was carried slopingly down to his head. In fine, after three days and three nights of incessant toil, the head of Billard was reached, and cleared of all surrounding matter. The instant that this took place, it was notified to those above by a cry, and the deafening shouts that were immediately raised, shewed what an assemblage had gathered around the place to learn the issue of the case. The deliverance took place exactly a quarter of an hour before eleven o'clock iu the morning of the

30th. When raised once more to the day light, every precaution was taken to prevent any bad effects from a change so sudden. lie was carried to a neighbouring house, with his body and head well wrapped up, and there he was laid in an apartment, from which the light was in a great measure excluded. After some spoonfuls of light broth and a little wine had been administered to him, he fell immediately asleep, never having tasted that blessing during his confinement. Before sleeping, he had spoken in such a way as to shew that his mind had recovered its tone. His pulse was weak but quick, beating 120 times in a minute ; his skin was cold, his thirst burning, and his tongue stuck almost to the roof of his mouth. While confined, he had eaten a portion of the leather front of his cap or bonnet, and he had even, he said, endeavoured to grind with his teeth a stone that lay before his mouth. Etienne Billard soon recovered. His imprisonment had not been so protracted as to render the vital heat difficult of restoration. His body, however, though not mangled or bruised, as it might have been expected to be, retained for a long time a feeling of dull pain, from the pressure that had been exerted upon it. þÿ Chamheds Miscellany.

Obstruction! to the use of flic Telescope. It h ;is been long known, liotli from theory and in practice, that the imperfect transparency of the earth's atmosphere, anil the unequal refraction which arises from differences tit' temperature, combine to set a limit to the use of high magnifying powers in our telescopes. Hitherto, however, the application of such high powers was checked liy the imperfections of the instruments themselves ; and it is only since the construction of Lord Itosse's telescope that astronomers have found that, in our damp and variable climate, it is only during a few days of the year that telescopes of such magnitude can use successfully the high magnifying powers which they are capable of hearing. Even iu a cloudless sky, when the stars are sparkling in the firmament, the astronomer is baffled by influences which are invisible, and while new planets and new satellites are being discovered by instruments comparatively small, the gigantic Polyphemus lies slumbering in his cave, blinded by thermal currents, more irresistible than the firebrand of Ulysses. As the astronomer, however, can not command a tempest to clear his atmosphere, nor a thunder storm to purify it, his only alternative is to remove his telescope to some southern climate, where no clouds disturb the serenity of the firmament, and no changes of temperature distract the emanations of the stars. A fact has been recently mentioned, which entitles us to anticipate great results from such a measure. The

Marquis of Ormonde is said to have seen from Mount Etna, with his naked eye, the satellites of Jupiter. If this be true, what discoveries may we not expect, even in Europe, from a large reflector working above the grosser strata of our atmosphere. This noble experiment of sending a large reflector to a southern climate has been but once made in the transported history of science. Sir John his his telescope and Herschel family to the south of Africa, and during a voluntary exile of four years' duration he enriched astronomy with many splendid discoveries. þÿ Sir David Brewster.

Skctt-li of Suwarow. The most able military commander that Russia has produced was in person miserably thin, and five feet one inch in height. A large mouth, pug nose, eyes commonly half shut, a few gray side locks, brought over the top of his bald crown, and a small unpowdered queue, the whole surmounted by a three-cornered felt hat ornamented with green fringe, composed the " head and front" of Field-marshal Suwarow ; but his eyes, when open, were piercing, and in battle they were said to be terrifically expressive. When any thing said or done displeased him, a wavy play of his deeplywrinkled forehead betrayed, or rather expressed, his disapproval. He had a philosophical contempt for dress, and might often be seen drilling his men in his shirt sleeves. It was only during the severest weather that he worecloth, hisoutergarments being usually of white serge turned up with green. These were the most indifferently made, as were his large, coarsely greased slouching boots; one of which he very commonly dispensed with, leaving his kneebnnd unbuttoned, and his stocking about bis heel. A huge sabre and a single order completed his ordinary costume ; but on grand occasions his field-marshal's uniform was covered with badges, and he was fondjof telling where and how he had won them. He often arose at midnight, and welcomed the first soldier he saw moving with a piercing imitation of the crowing of a cock, in compliment to his early rising. It is said that in the first Polish war,

knowing a spy was in the camp, he issued orders for an attack at cock-crow, and the enemy expecting it in the morning , were cut to pieces at nine at night þÿ Suwarow having turned out the troops an hour before by his well-known cry. T'he evening before the storm of Ismail, he informed his columns þÿ " To-morrow morning, an hour before daybreak I mean to get up. 1 shall then dress and wash myself, then say my prayers, and then give one good cock-crow, and capture Ismail." When Segur asked him if he never took off his clothes at night, he replied " No ! when I get lazy, and want to have a comfortable sleep, I generally take oft' one spur." Buckets of cold water were thrown over him before he dressed, and bis table was served at seven or eight o'clock with sandwiches and various messes which Duboscagc describes as " des ragouts Kosaks detestab'.es to which men paid "the mouth honor, which they would fain deny, but dare not," lest Suwarow should consider them effeminate. He had been very sickly in his youth, but by spare diet and cold bathing had strengthened and hardened himself into first-rate condition. þÿ Harped s Magazine. West India Maii. From the St. Thomas Times, April 20. British Consulate Santo Domingo.

The undersigned, Her Britannic Maþÿjesty Consul s to the Dominican Republic, begs to bring publicly to the notice of the commerce and of Shippers by British vessels in general, that the attention to the following regulations is requisite previous to his being empowered of despatching a vessel at the Consulate. 1. Every British vessel arriving at this port or in the roads without, whether with cargo or in ballast, has to he reported at the Consulate within fortyeight hours of her arrival, otherwise the master subjects himself to a fine of Five Pounds Sterling (7 & 8 Vic, I. Cap. 112, $ 53.) 2. The nature and value of the cargo of every British vessel entering from abroad whether the said vessel is only in part or fully loaded, has to he declared at the Consulate on the deposition of the þÿship p s apers. 3. It is requisite that before the þÿship s papers can be returned to the master on the departure of the vessel, a manifest of the cargo and its value be deposited at this Consulate. If the vessel lie hound to a British port, the manifest has to he delivered in duplicate, one of which the master has to sign before the Consul, declaring that the manifest is a correct statement of all the merchandize he has loaded on hoard of his vessel. Forms of the manifest may be procured at the Consulate on application. 4. Every British vessel, for whatsoever port she may be destined, has to produce at this Consulate her clearance from the Customhouses here, and the pass from the Commandant of Arms, as
a proof that he has paid the duties and dues of the Republic; in the absence of

these documents her þÿship p s apers cannot be delivered. 5. All Fees at the British Consulate are by Act of Parliament to he paid in Silver Dollars at the rate of 4s. 2d. each, payment to he made on the delivery of any document emanating from this Consulate, as it cannot be expected that the Consul is to keep a book to enter the same for a future settlement. 6. The hours for transacting Consular business at the office, are from 11 þÿo clock in the morning, to 3 þÿo clock in the afternoon. The undersigned solicits the attention of the Commerce to these regulations which are in force at every British Consulate; the compliance with which will greatly facilitate the despatch of vessels and other Consular business, and prevent unnecessary delays. ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK, Consul.

New fork Crystal Palace. From the present appearance of this far-famed structure, we should suppose that it will not be completed before the middle of May, or the first of June. The frame work, however, is nearly finished, with the exception of the roof, which yet remains to be put on. The front part, facing the Sixth avenue, is more advanced than any other portion of the building. Here the glass is already put in the iron window frames, and the painters are at work. The columns, which will be soon finished, are very handsome indeed ; and on each one may lie seen mounted about half a dozen men, busily engaged in drilling, hammering, and filing. The flooring has just been commenced, at which a large number of our best mechanics are engaged at work. The Reservoir which overlooks this beautiful edifice, and commands a fine view of the building, is daily crowded with visitors of both sexes, watching with pleasure the progress of a structure which for beauty, has never been equalled. No doubt the contractors are using their utmost endeavours in order that it may be opened on the first of May. We hope that they will not disappoint the people, and that the character of the American mechanics, who are famed for promptness, energv, and talent, will not sulfer by " the slowness of the contractors. þÿ Nat York Herald , A/trili).

The Verbena. M i:thoii for preparing and administering the þÿ Verbena for the cure of Black Vomit and Yellow Fever: þÿ þÿ A sufficient quantity of Verbena leaves to be collected to fill a common mortar, and pounded, with a few spoonfulls of cold water. The mass to be squeezed and strained through a coarse towel, and three tea spoonfulls of common salt added to a tumbler full of the liquid. 'File dose is 4 table spoonfulls every three hours for a youth of from 10 to 12 years of age, and in proportion for persons of other ages ; the mixture to be given luke warm. Injections of the same mixture to be used at the same times as the doses, but with an equal quantity of warm water added, and instead of salt, to be made slightly sweet with loaf sugar. These doses and injections to he used for three days, and as much cold water given to the patient as he may desire to drink. The mixture is purgative, though the patient may probably vomit after taking it two or three times. The first evacuations will be black, with clotted portions of blood, and probably with blood in succeeding stools, and then on the 2nd and 3rd days the evacuations will resume a natural

3 ® It 5E A'HS. color. After the 3rd day, Seidlitz Powders should be given freely. The diet should be sago, panada, and chicken soup, at short intervals. The drink should be solely cold water. The foregoing is the statement of Mrs. Orfila, as taken and translated from her Spanish, and on which all the medical practitioners here have acted with complete success. þÿ Bolivar, 28th February, 1853. þÿ Kenneth þÿMathison.

IVi/mer and Smith's European Times, April 1, 1853.. Great efforts seem to be making at Constantinople to put the finances in order by means of a bank. Several schemes have been proposed to the Sultan, but nothing definitive has been decided upon.

By the submarine telegraph we are informed that a conspiracy has been discovered at Berlin. Twenty persons have been arrested, eighty houses searched, and arms and ammunitions have been found. From what we hear we fear that the efforts of the democratic party throughout Europe are incessant, and that fresh troubles may lie expected It is said that the Emperor of Morocco is dying, and that his death will be a signal for a terrible crisis. The Austrian Government has issued an amnesty as it is well called of the þÿ þÿInnocents. Such as it is, the Mayor of Milan has made the most of it, and at Mantua it has caused much satisfaction. þÿ'I lie government, however, continues to expel the political refugees with great rigour, and no mercy is shown to the Hungarians. As we anticipated, the Pope hesitates about proceeding to Paris. A delay is a virtual refusal. Death of the Di ke of Padua. þÿ The Paris papers announce the death of the Duke of Padua. The duke, who was 78 years of age, was a member of the Senate. He was allied to the family of the Emperor, his father having been a cousin-german of the grandmother of Napoleon III. He entered the army at an early age ; was a captain in 1798, was wounded at the assault of Jaffa, and left for dead at San Jean þÿd Acre. Napoleon named him General of Brigade on the field of battle of Friedland. lie was soon created Duke of Padua, and at Esling was named General of Division, in the room of General Espagne, who was killed at the commencement of the
battle. He was present at Lutzen and Bautzes, defended Leipsic when attacked during the armistice, and fought bravely in the campaign of France.

From the London Times, April 1, 1853. FRANCE. PARIS, March 31, 6 r. m. The deputation from the merchants of London dined with the Emperor yesterday, and to-day the deputation of the Pacific and Atlantic Junction Company were admitted to His þÿMajesty table. s A free pardon has been granted to 257 military convicts ; the punishment of 394 convicts has been reduced.

PARIS, March 30, 6 p. m. Yesterday, the Emperor granted an audience to a deputation of the English company who propose joining the Atlantic with the Pacific ocean. The Ambassadors from Peru and New Grenada joined the deputation, and were also received by the Emperor. Sir Charles Fox, the president of the company, ad-

dressed the Emperor in the following terms : þÿ þÿ þÿ Sire, In approaching your august throne ray first duty is to tender to your Imperial Majesty the cordial expression of the respectful gratitude of the Directors of the Atlantic and Pacific Junction Company for the prompt kindness with which your Majesty has condescended to grant þÿ an audience to their deputation. The rapid increase of commercial navigation round Cape-Horn has now, for some years, attracted the practical attention of men of business to that which had previously been considered a merely speculative object of scientific inquiry. I mean the necessity for a direct passage for ships between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, across the isthmus which unites North and South America. þÿ In the year 1851 my attention was directed by Dr. Cullen, who had himself traversed the isthmus, to the route across Darien, between Porte Escoses and San Miguel, which his experience had led him to consider the best. þÿ On examining the Admiralty charts, which, as your Imperial Majesty is well aware, are very detailed and accurate, I was able to ascertain that the line proposed to me was the only one which could enjoy the advantage of a sufficient natural harbour at each end ; that the length of the passage would not exceed 60 kilometres ; and that the only question to be decided was, whether the engineering difficulties of the ground were such as to prevent within a reasonable expenditure the construction of a channel of suffi-

cient width and depth to satisfy the requirements of all nations. Iu conjunction, therefore, with Mr. Brassey and several friends, I commissioned Mr. Gisborne and Mr. Fordo, civil engineers, to examine the isthmus, and I have had the satisfaction to ascertain from their report that it is perfectly possible to cut a channel 1 60 feet wide and HO feet deep, without locks, between the two harbours which 1 have mentioned, at an expense by no means out of proportion to the objects to be attained and to the revenue which may reasonably be expected. We have accordingly formed a company to carry out this object. þÿ At the outset of our investigations, and as soon as we had obtained the necessary concession from the local authority of New Grenada, we deemed it right, as a matter of courtesy, to offer to the United States a share in the undertaking We have throughout received the cordial approbation of Her Britannic þÿMajesty G þÿ s overnment Our next step is, with the full consent of that Government, to solicit the patronage and support of your Imperial Majesty. France, as one of the great maritime Powers, has an evident interest in this great question of a junction between the two oceans. France, who owes so much to your Imperial Majesty, will, we believe, be grateful to you, Sire, for granting your Impeþÿ rial countenance and support to our undertaking and in the name of this deputation and of the company whom we have the honour to represent, I venture to hope for this support with perfect

confidence, because we know that your Imperial Majesty, not only as the chief of this great nation, but also by your personal knowledge of the subject, is pre-eminently qualified to appreciate the object which we have in view and the means which we have þÿadopted. The Emperor replied in English as follows : þÿ þÿ Gentlemen, I received with the liveliest interest the intelligence of the formation of a great company for the junction of the two oceans, I have no doubt that you will succeed in an undertaking which must render so important a service to the commerce of the whole world, since such eminent men are placed at the head of your company. I have long appreciated all the advantages of a junction between the two seas, and when I was in England I endeavoured to draw the attention of scientific men to this subject You may, therefore, rest assured, gentlemen, that you will meet with all the support from me which such noble efforts þÿdeserve. The þÿcompany s report, plans, and maps were then laid before the Emperor, who examined them with particular attention. Sir Charles Fox presented the members of the deputation, and His Majesty addressed to each of them the most gracious expressions. When the deputation withdrew the Emperor said: þÿ I am happy to have seen your honourable deputation the very day after having received the one which, on the part of the merchants of London, expressed to me þÿ ments in favour of peace sentiments with which the most friendly sentimy own feelings have always been in complete
þÿaccord.

England will be again lashing itself into a fury against the slave system of America, and into a perfect storm of enthusiasm for the gifted authoress. Nothing shows more clearly þÿ the extraordinary influence of Mrs. þÿStowe s land, Uncle þÿTom, than the appearance so soon after its publication of a þÿ þÿKey to the work. This fact bears testimony to the earnest nature of the questions that have been suggested by the remarkable fiction, and the necessity that existed of satisfying them. For our parts, we think that the necessity existed more in America than here. Englishmen have made up their minds upon the subject of slavery, and could find all the needful proofs of the correctness of the delineation in the works of English travellers. It is in America only that Mrs. Stowe has been made the object of vituperation, and where the truth of her scenes has been contested. If it were possible to feel sorry for the triumph of truth, we should say we were sorry that the partisans 1 finite ages the emancipation of a race. When General

There they are; in their own dirty deformity, not toned down artistically by the hand of Kennis, or brought into something like harmony with surrounding objects, but chewing, spitting, blaspheming, kicking, murdering with horrible, unrelieved reality. The first part of M rs. þÿStowe book, s which is devoted to the purpose of identifying her characters with real prototypes, must always stand as an unwell as of her wonderful impeachable guarantee of her truth and power as an artist. Equally honesty, as successful has she been in the second part, which þÿcon sistsofa review of the laws upon the subject of slavery and anexaminationof various cases in which the law has been exercised. It is clear from this examination that masters do, now and then, kill slaves by the torture 'hat the fact of so killing slaves is not of itself þÿhel d presumption of murder in slave jurisprudence, and that the slave in the act of resistance to his master may always be killed. It is, however, in the third part of the work that the thoughtful Englishman will find the most matter for consideration. We can only point to one or two important conclusions to which a perusal of this very portion of the work cannot fail to lead the reader. The first is, that slavery is not only a curse to the slaves themselves, but a source of infinite degradation to all

but the higher orders amongst the whites. With the exception of the slave proprietors themselves, the white ! and þÿdegraded imputation in the stave states are as a class, uneducated þÿ more heathenish, degraded, and miserable than the slaves þÿthemselves, says the authoress. This is accounted for very simply. The great size of the plantations makes any system of common school education þÿimpossible the same causes set hindrances ot the idea of labour in the way of religious teaching, and the degradation resulting from enslaving the work- j ing class prevents the establishment of a ' respectable ! middle working class. The only standard of respect- | ability is being able to live without work. A large j planter buys his carpenter, or cooper, or mason when he wants one. How can a free labourer of either class hope, then, for employment, or for respect if he obtains it. The lower class of whites thus grow in up idleness, vice, dirt, and misery of all sorts. Strange to say, how- | ever, these men are the most ferocious advocates of slavery. They are despised by the upper classes, and they find a miserable pleasure in having a class below them on whom they may exercise their contempt. Abolition would deprive them of this pleasure, and they therefore oppose it with an energy that stops at nothing. The leading men take advantage of this feeling, and use the cry of þÿ þÿAbolitionism to urge this ferocious mob of degraded whites to any excess in defence of their miserable privileges.

Is there a man teaching his negroes to read ? The mob is started upon him þÿ he must promise to give it up, or leave the state. Does a man at a public hotel-table express his approbation of some anti-slavery work ? Up come the police and arrest him for seditious language, and on the heels of the police, thronging round the þÿjustices office, come the ever ready mob, men with clubs and bowie-knives, swearing that they will have his þÿheart s blood. Still more important, however, than the degradation of the whites in a few stave states, is the fact that as far as can be seen, the present tendency of the progress of America is not only to strengthen the institution of | slavery but to extend it. Slavery, Mrs. Stowe shows, was really dying out until the extension of stave territory, the opening of a great southern slave-market, and the consequent organisation of a great internal stave , trade, put energy into the system. In Delaware, Mary- Virginia, and Kentucky slave labour was found to be entirely unproductive. Kentucky only preserved slavery in the state by a majority of one in the legislature. In Virginia and Maryland public opinion was equally strong, and there was every chance that the institution would have fallen by its own weight. Suddenly came the acquisition of stave territory in the | south, and it was discovered that although stave labour

was unprofitable in the north, it was well worth while þÿauthoress s to breed slaves for the south. This terrible trade now finds its greatest supporters in the states where it was not long ago on the point of perishing. America has paid for the purchase of new territory by the retention ot the greatest blot on her social system. The extension of her sovereignty lias deferred perhaps for inde-

An interesting but painful subject of consideration is presented to us in the numerous examples of the culpable assistance that religious bodies of various denominations have afforded to the cause of slavery by the preaching of their ministers. The authoress has collected an appalling body of evidence bearing on this subject John Bull will, we suppose, exhibit a degree of excitement on the arrival of the authoress that will lead Brother Jonathan to express a doubt or two of his ! sanity It is very probable, we confess, that the thing may be overdone; but, after all, the enthusiasm excited by the presence of the authoress of a most succesful book written in the great cause of humanity, is every whit as respectable as the same amount of enthusiasm displayed at the advent of a songstress, and much more 1 healthy. From the St. Thomas Times, April 23. COLONIAL PENNY POSTAGE. The arrival of every mail brings fresh proofs of the deep interest which the colonies take in the projected reduction of rate and alterations in the system of colonial postage. A petition to the House of Commons has just arrived from Trinidad, signed by 112 of the leading merchants and planters in the colony, praying the legislature to extend the system of prepaid penny postage to that and every other portion of the empire. The petitioners say, truly, that cheap postal communication with England, as the centre of the commercial world, would be one of the surest means of binding the colonies and the mother country together by feelings of mutual interest. Similar petitions have been sent from Tobago, addressed to the Lords and Commons, signed by the Speaker and many of the members of the General Assembly, and by nearly all the leading proprietors, planters, and merchants in the colony. Another petition is on its way from Halifax signed by the members of the Executive and Legislative Councils of the Province, by the members ofthe House of Assembly, the Chief Justice, the Bishops, and by all the principal merchants of the city of Halifax. A fifth is coming from St. John, New Brunswick, originated by the Chamber of Commerce of that place, and numerously and respectably signed. Petitions are also announced as being in course of signature at Antigua, the Cape, Guiana, Grenada, Hong Kong, Jamaica, Montreal, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Si. Thomas, and Singapore, and may all be ex-

We, the undersigned, merchants, bankers, traders, and others, of London, feel ourselves called upon, at this time, publicly to express the concern with which we learn, through various channels of information, that an impression exists in the minds of the people of France, that feelings of an unfriendly character are entertained towards them by the people of England. We think it right emphatically to declare, that we believe no such feelings exist on the part of the English people towards the people of France. We believe the welfare of both nations to be closely interwoven, as well in a mutually advantageous and extending commercial intercourse, as in a common participation in all the improvements of art and science. Rejoicing in the reflection, that nearly forty years have passed since the final cessation of hostilities between France and England, wo record our conviction, that European wars should be remembered only to be deplored, for the sacrifice of life and treasure with which they were attended þÿ the hindrances they interposed to all useful enterprise and social advancement þÿ the angry and unchristian feelings which they evoked in their progress þÿ and the heavy financial burdens which they left behind them at their close : considerations which supply the most powerful motives to every individual in the European community to avoid, and to oppose, by every means in his

power, whatever may tend to cause the recurrence of such evils. We desire to remark that, if in that expression of opinion on public questions which the press of j this country is accustom ed to exercise it is found occasionally to speak with apparent harshness of the Government or the institutions of other States, the same is not to be understood in a spirit of national hostility, or as desiring to give offence. Wo feel that with the internal policy or mode of Government which the French nation may think good to adopt for itself it is not for British subjects to interfere, further than heartily to desire that it may result in peace and happiness to all interested therein. We conclude this declaration by proclaiming our earnest desire for the long continuance of cordiality and goodwill between Frenchmen and Englishmen, our determination to do all in our power to uphold the same, and our fervent hope that the inhabitants of both nations may in future only vie with each other in cultivating the arts of peace, and in extending the sources of social improvement, for their common benefit. London, March, 1853.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Ads. Sir, It will be remembered, that in the month of January 1852 an election of three members to fill up the vacancies in the Burgher Council of this Island took place in our town. These members were returned for one year ; their term of office consequently expired in January last. It was as a matter of course expected by every body, that at the expiration of that term, a new election would have taken place. But it was explained, that as the election was intended for an indefinite time, the members would continue in office, until the reorganization of our communal relations was effected þÿ unless the withdrawal or absence of any member made a new election necessary. Now, Sir, without entering at present in the question whether the rights of the Electors of this Island can be explained away, I would claim your attention to the crisis at hand. þÿ The three old þÿmembers of the Burgher Council having retired or tendered their resignations, a new election becomes necessary. What will be done? Will the election be partial or general? Speculation is rife on the subject. The prevailing opinion is that a general election is imperatively requisite. If the Electors be called on to elect three members in lieu of six, it could not he expected, that as the members returned by them last year have been continued in office after the expiration of the term for which they were elected, the Electors would respond to the appeal. Besides a partial election

would lead to an anomaly to he deprecated. There would he three members returned by the Electors and three not elected by them, for it is incontrovertible, that these members were returned for one year, which has expired. Our political institutions are so few, and our rights so circumscribed, that we cannot with apathy see them diminished or reduced within narrower bounds. St. Thomas 29lh April 1853. I am, Sir, Your obedient servant, An Ucclor.

A statement hits been published on the motion of Mr. Hume, showing the extent of the irregularities of the West India mail steamers during the past two years. It appears that during 1851 they were behind time in their arrivals at Southampton an average of 4| days, that on one occasion the mail was overdue I I days, and that in no instance did it arrive at its proper date. In 1852 their average behind time was 35 days; one case of delay amounted to 15 days, and another to 14. Two instances, however, took place of arrivals two days before the appointed time, and one instance of an arrival at the due date On the other side, the departures from St. þÿThomas s were only punctual in four cases during 1851, and in three cases in 1852. Considering that the time allowed before a vessel is officially regarded as þÿ þÿdue is always of itself sufficient to leave an ample margin for slow sailing, the figures thus presented furnish a remarkable illustration of the results of a monopoly which has recently been fastened upon the country at an expense of, £270, 000 per annum for an additional eleven years, to say nothing of the high fares and general discomforts which have formed the subject of complaints and protests until it has been felt useless to continue them. A memorial has been addressed to the Admiralty by the merchants of Bristol on the inconveniences sustained from the repeated failures of the Royal West India Mail Company to fulfil the engagements of their time tables. The memo- I

rialists state that the failures in question are so notorious as to render it unnecessary to specify particular grievances, but they point to the recent fact, þÿ that the steamer due on the 7th February last did not arrive till the 9th of March, and that the steamer due on the 1st March did not arrive till the þÿ8th. Finally, it is observed, þÿ that the statement in defence of the company inserted in the Times, of the 12th u It., virtually admits the irregularities complained of, and that the excuses therein set forth are not such as should exonerate þÿthem.

Ingenious Device of Belgian Smi g lf.rs. þÿ The French Custom-house officers stationed at Wallers have just made an important seizure. A cart drawn by four horses, and apparently laden with coal, came from the Belgian frontier, and drew up at the Customhouse to be examined and obtain the usual pass. One of the officers, in verifying the contents of the cart, put his hands on what he thought to be an enormous block of coal, and to bis great surprise found that he could lift it. without difficulty. This led to a minute examination, when what appeared to be large masses of that combustible turned out to be boxes ingeniously coated over with coal, which was attached to them by cement. The cart in this way contained about 2090 kilogrammes of tobacco, and several thousands of excellent cigars. The cart and horses were also seized.

A friend visiting Naples lias sent us some interesting particulars of the opening of a Roman tomb, one among the many which, together with the ruins of a Grecian temple, have been lately discovered at the ancient city ofCuma. A labourer, going to plant trees, struck on stone work, and so it came to light. The þÿking brother, s Count of Syracuse, on whose estate it was, set | men to work, and is still prosecuting the search with interest and eagerness. The writer goes on I city. He has, it is said, succeeded in constructto say that one hundred men are at work on it, and the affair is making a noise here. Asking leave of the prince to attend, we were invited to his palace to see what he had of it there, and next day, by appointment, we met him at the vineyard at Ouma, where the tombs are found, and spent ! and a company lias subscribed the means of giving four hours with him overlooking the workmen. After examining the site of the temple, called of Diana þÿ a statue of the goddess having been found there þÿ we saw various other ruins of houses, tombs, unshapen large masses of Roman brickwork which lie about the ground, remains of the ancient city ofCuma. After going down into one tomb, in which are columbaria or small niches all round, to hold cinerary urns with the burnt bones, we took up our station near the score or more of men who were digging where there was reason to expect a tomb. Experience guiding them, they demolished a tree, and shovelling off the soil we presently came to stonework that sounded hollow.

This proved to be the mouth of the tomb, and clearing fast away, and picking and breaking one of the large tufo stones that formed it, we made a hole big enough to creep through. Conceive my interest at the moment ; we found ourselves in a dry arched ! chamber or vault, constructed of solid and large pieces of stone, say 1 2 feet by 10 feet, an arched I doorway of entrance on one side walled up ; round the other three sides, partitions of strong stonework, raised above the floor, of length and width to receive the bodies. Raking up the loose sand usually found in such receptacles, and the stucco that had fallen down from the walls and roof, which had been thickly plastered with it, we i soon came to human bones, ivory combs (one precisely shaped and made like those in present J use), parts of an streaked bottle, luccrnse, ivory flute, alabaster smelling- glass and terra-cotta buttons, small elegant vases of glass and terra cotta, but no money, though they found in the mouth of one skeleton lately a coin of Diocletian, proving that the tomb was used down to his reign. The Rev. Dr. Tyng. We know few men who can do so large an amount of public duty in the Church, and yet do it so well, as the Rev. Rector of St. þÿGeorge s, New York. Some of our readers may have seen tin article travelling the rounds of the press, in which the Dr. is represented sis having said some very foolish things respecting spiritual lappings. The article alledges that he had contended for the þÿ spiritual origin of the manifestations that lie þÿ admitted the facts, and repudiated the idea of there being some new developements of magnetic or electric forces that he announced that there þÿ were mediums among the communicants of his church that he had þÿ himself personally wrestled with this adversary almost incessantly for three weeks þÿpast; that þÿ the if annoyance continued to increase, lie should he obliged to relinquish his þÿministry. As we were not prepared to believe that the excitement of New York life, or the Lenten services of St. þÿGeorge s Church, had prepared our old friend and fellow labourer for an insane hospital, we passed the article by, as one of those lying announcements with which this monstrous system of collusion and fraud is so heavily freighted. From the St. Thomas Times, May 1 1, 1853. COLONIAL. barbados. "Captain Philip Drake Evans, late of the Schooner Sally Evans, was tried at Barbados, on the 8th instant, for the

murder of the Steward of that vessel. (Thomas Walcott), while lying in Carlisle bay on the 15th June last. The Jury acquitted him for a the murder, but brought in verdict charge of against him of" manslaughter." The judge, in sentencing the prisoner, said þÿ " ' Philip Drake Evans, the jury to which your case was submitted, atter a protracted, careful, no and impartial vestigation, have, doubt, in the con- inscientious discharge of their duty, declared you innocent of the crime of murder, and guilty of the lesser crime of manslaughter. Far be it from me to find fault with their verdict; I am bound to believe that that verdict is the conscientious conviction of those who could alone pronounce upon the issue referred to them ; but I cannot but say, that if your case is not one of murder, it is as near murder as any case that ever was tried in this court; at least, since I have been sitting here. I am sure if your previous character be that which it has been described by your Counsel, who was prepared to put in testimonials in proof of his statement in this respect, nothing that 1 could now say can add to that, bitter remorse which you now feel. Arou certainly have had a narrow escape of your life; for, assuredly, if the jury had found you guilty of the higher charge, I know of no circumstances which would have warranted me in arresting the arm of the law. In your case, it is my duty to pass upon you the highest sentence that the law sanctions for the worst and most aggravated form of the crime of

manslaughter. The law directs that any person guilty of manslaughter may, at the discretion of the Court, be transported beyond the seas for his natural life, or for any term not less than seven years, or be imprisoned, with or without hard labour, for any term not exceeding four years. The whole extent of the imprisonment 1 am warranted in passing upon you is, 1 think, far from being a just and sufficient punishment for your crime; I shall therefore pass upon you the highest sentence I am authorized to award, and although it cannot be carried out þÿ (and, for the sake of the outraged laws of society, more is the pity) þÿ I am nevertheless induced to pass it in the punishment hope that it might be measure in some commuted for a proportionate to the grave, and, 1 repeat it, highly aggravated character of your offence. The sentence of the Court upon you is that you be transported for the term of your natural life.'"

There is but one way in which it has occurred to the Government that they might entertain a sanguine hope of being able, at very slight charge to this country, perhaps at no charge, to confer material benefit on the West Indies ; and that is a way which, if it can be effected, will, I am sure, command the approbation of this House, because it is by enabling them to economise the heavy expenditure of their own governments þÿ (hear, hear) þÿ a heavy and now in many cases almost a ruinous expenditure. (Hear.) In the case of Jamaica, for example, there is a public debt, the minimum rate of interest upon which is 6 per cent., and the maximum 10 per cent., the capital of the debt amounting to about .£500,000 ; and if it were possible for the Government to induce the Assembly of Jamaica to amend the vicious constitution of that island, and to place it upon a foundation that would give scope for a strict control over expenditure, her Majesty's Government would then be disposed to recommend to this House to employ the credit of this country in a guarantee for the island of Jamaica. (Hear, hear.) I do not now inquire whether that would entail a charge upon you ; I believe

it would entail none. I would be the first to assert that there should be the utmost jealousy as to the interposition of the credit of this country between debtors and creditors out of this country þÿ (hear, hear) þÿ but, considering all that has happened to the West Indies, considering the effect that British legislation has had in precipitating their difficulties, I do believe that if we were able to point out a prospect of great and effectual relief to Jamaica, to be indirectly obtained through an effectual reform in its government, this House would look with a generous and a considerate eye upon any proposal for using the credit of this country in the manner that I have mentioned. (Hear, hear.) That refers to Jamaica, which presents at this moment by far the most urgent case of distress among the West India colonies. (Hear, hear.) I am not sure that there is any other among those colonies which would be in a condition to request a similar interposition. (Hear, hear.) If they did, it would depend upon the case they showed. I do not think it likely that such a case will arise ; all I mean to say at the present moment is that the door would not be absolutely shut against them, (Hear, hear.)
