A Rival to þÿTea. The Leaves of the Coffee Plant. þÿ The Singapore Free Press recommends the use of the coffee leaf as a substitute for the berry. The sensible writer appears to be an English planter of the Dutch settlement of Paclang, in Sumatra, where the coffee plant has been cultivated for several generations, and where it is now produced in larger quantity and of better quality than in any country of the Malayan Islands, Java excepted. The coffee plant is an ever-green large shrub, which yields a profusion of leaves, and bears fruit for about twenty years. The leaf, and even the twigs, have, in a minor degree, the same stimulating and exhilarating property as the berry, and its habitual use by the natives of the country, agricultural Malays of very simple habits, and little amenable to innovation, shows that they at least find the coffee leaf to make a wholesome and agreeable beverage. The introduction of this article into our consumption would, we cannot help thinking, be a benefit to the poor and to our colonial planters. In order to render coffee leaves marketable for European Consumption, we fancy the best mode of preparation will consist in subjecting them to the same kind of manipulation as tea undergoes, and for this purpose it would probably be expedient, at first, to employ, for instruction, Chinese skilled in the art, such men as Mr. Fortune lately brought from the

northern provinces of China to Upper India. The leaves of coffee, neither fleshy nor succulent, are even more easily dried than those of tea; and being larger and more abundant, while the plant itselfis more easily reared than tea, and embraces a much wider geographical range, it is certain they might be sold at a lower price than the poorest Bohea. It may be added that the leaves so prepared would not be amenable to the charge of adulteration so often urged against the ground berry. The subject is worth the attention of planters, traders, and consumers.

J\ Talc of flic l;iNiuii«<. Antonio Jomei.li was the best artisan of his profession in Naples He was a worker in bronze, a department of the arts for which the Italians have been long celebrated. Antonio's skill bad gained him reputation and abundant employment, and from his workshop had issued the greater number of the candelabras and other metallic ornaments to be found in the palaces of Naples. The brouze-worker had grown rich by his occupation, but the usual concomitant of riches, pride, he had eschewed. He still laboured away at bis trade, with bis own hands, confining his personal attention chiefly to be finer and more difficult articles which hi! was required to fabricate, while men in his employ manufactured, in a large and separate workshop, the common articles of the trade. One evening, as Antonio sat alone in the little apartment where he pursued his labours, lie was informed that a lady wished to speak with him He desired her to bo admitted immediately. The visitor was a female of tall and stately form and carriage, with a dark thick veil thrown over her head and face, so as to prevent the bronze-worker from discerning the features beneath The lady, for such her dress betokened her to be, did not speak until the servant who had admitted her had left the room for some moments. Turning, then, her glance from the door to Jomelli, and seating herself in the chair which he had placed for her, she said, in a voice which her hearer thought the most sweet and mellifluous that had ever fallen

upon his ear, but which seemed strangely agitated, uttered : You work in bronze þÿ considering ' the common-place matter which it you can make bronze ornaments of all kinds ? Is it so ?' ' It is, lady,' replied the artisan ; ' and I shall be proud to execute anything of that nature for yo«'r ' Yes, yes,' said the lady ; ' I wish a piece of work done. I have a statue of great value þÿ the statue of a conqueror and king þÿ done by the hand of a first-rate sculptor. It is perfect in every respect but one : it wants a chaplet of flowers to adorn its temples ; and this is what I wish you to make for it.' ' Is the statue of bronze, madainc ?' was the artist's question. ' No,' replied the lady ; ' it is white, of pure marble, and you must paint the chaplet of that colour when you have made it.' ' What form then, lady, do you choose it to be of?' said the artist ; ' what shape or pattern shall the ornaments have? But, perhaps, I had better see the statue, and measure the dimensions of the head.' ' No, no,' exclaimed the visitor hurriedly ; ' it will not be necessary. I have looked upou it so often, that I can tell you perfectly well how large it is. Your own head is very near it; yes, you cannot go wrong, if you fit the chaplet to your own head.' ' And the fashion of the ornaments, madam ?' ' Let it be heavy, very heavy,' replied the lady, sinking ' Let it be her very voice to a concentrated whisper. weighty, that it may not fall oft' easily ; and make it jagged, and full of spikes in-

side, that it may adhere to the brows of the statue.' 1 Still, lady, the band should be wrought in some ornamental fashion,' said Antonio. ' but, Do remember, ' that as you please,' was the lady's reply ; it is to be heavy, and full of spikes ; and forget not that it is to be painted white, so as to resemble flowers. And now, when will it be finished ?' ' A Oh, few days !' days, ' in a few cried the lady vehemently, ris- madam,' said the artist. ing from her chair at the same time ; 'it must be ready to-morrow evening, sir ! I must have it tomorrow.' ' I cannot do justice to the chaplet, lady,' said tone ; ' the ornamental part' the bronze-worker, astonished at her violence of

' I care not for any ornaments,' was the hasty reply ; ' make it as I have directed ; and to-morrow I must have it, because þÿ because I am to have a party, and wish the statue to be then ornamented.' ' Well, madam,' said the artist resignedly, ' I shall do my endeavour. Aud whither shall I have the honour of sending it.' ' I shall call for it myself at this hour to-morrow, and shall pay what you will for it. Remember what I have said þÿ heavy, and set with spikes.' With these words the lady departed, leaving on Jomelli's mind the impression that, fanciful as many of his former employers had been, this new one was the most flighty of all. On the evening following that on which this singular order was given to the artist Jouiolli, all the grandees and fashionables of Naples, and not a small part of the populace, were on the move towards the splendid theatre of San Carlos. A piece of great interest was to be performed, and the prima donna, who was young and beautiful, was the exquisite vocalist Signora Marina. The lady had but lately been appointed to take the part of chief singer, and had therefore superseded one who had formerly been her acknowledged superior þÿ Madame Gambrici. Considering the comparative humiliation which Madame Cambrici had endured in the eyes of the Neapolitans, it was not to be supposed that she would on the present occasion make her appearance iu the house. But few knew the real character of their former favourite. To the astonishment, and, we should add, the delight of the audience, Gambrici

attended, as if for the purpose of acknowledging the merits and gracing the triumph of the inimitable Marina. She appeared in one of the most conspicuous parts of the theatre þÿ the front corner of the upper box overhanging the stage. Before the opera commenced, the audience called out the name of their former favourite, G ambrici , and cheered her for her seen: ing freedom from jealousy in being present on such an occasion. The object of their attention, however, appeared to be abashed by the plaudits she had raised, and moved not a muscle in reply, but, half covered by her veil, sat with her eye fixed on the stage. The piece at length commenced, the young prima donna appeared, and the cheers were long and loud. Marina had not been overpraised, either as regarded her person or performance. Kvery step which she took across the stage elicited admiration, for her movements were like those of a sylph ; every note which she uttered drew forth applause, for her voice was sweet and strong as Philomel's. In every song of the piece she was successful, but attention and expectation were chiefly rivetted upon one song, once Gambrici's master-piece. Marina at length reached this part of the opera ; she was then alone upon the stage. She sang the first verse, and the audience were in raptures. She sang the second, and crowns of flowers were scattered upon the stage, while even Gambrici was seen by the audience to applaud. She sang the third and last, and in doing so chanced to stand immediately below

Gambrici's box. To the delight of the spectators, Gambrici rose at that moment with a large crown of flowers, and waving it in the air, threw it down on the young Marina's head. The crown bounded from the singer's brow, and rolled along the stage, while Marina herself fell prostrate on the boards. She gave one scream, and never spoke or moved again. The flower-covered crown or ehaplet was the heavy bronze one made by Jomclli, and one of the spikes had entered the victim's brain ! It would be impossible to describe the confusion, the horror, the execrations that ensued. Gambrici having gratified her malignant revenge, seemed coutcntcu that she should pay for it with her life. She had slain her rival, the unfortunate Marina, and was satisfied. Dreadful must those passions have been, which could prompt the execution of so unhallowed a deed. Looking around her with calm and reckless indifference, she did not make the slightest attempt to escape, and was forthwith seized, and speedily brought to justice. Antonio Joinelli was confronted with her for form's sake, and avowed having made for her the fatal wreath. It has only to be added, that she did not die on the scaffold, but put an end to her existence by poison in the prison where she was confined. þÿ Chamber's Miscellany.

Tlir Mew York Exhibition. ( From the London Times.) Besides flic Karl of Ellesmere, Sir Charles Lyell, and Mr. Dilke, the Royal Commission which is about to he issued for the American International Exhibition, will, we understand, embrace the names of Professor O. Wilson, Mr. Whit-

8 IK S Ui © ATI 3 , worth, and Mr. Wallis. It will thus consist of six members, and form a body well calculated not only worthily to represent this country on the other side of the Atlantic, but to bring back, in the shape of official reports, the results of the approaching industrial display. The nobleman who is placed at the head of the Commission is thoroughly qualified to pronounce a judgment upon the merits of the Fine Arts' section, while he unites with a highly cultivated taste the prestige of rank and wealth. Science, especially in the departments of raw produce and mineralogy, could not find in this country a worthier representative than Sir Charles Lyell ; and Mr Dilke, the least rewarded, and certainly not the least valuable member of our own Executive Committee in Hyde-park, by his practical good sense, his business habits, and his experience, may fairly be expected to stamp the new Commission with a useful as well as a merely dignified character. Professor Wilson is favourably known to the public from the attention which he has paid to scientific agriculture, and it may be anticipated that at New York he will find the materials for much useful information to his own countrymen in that and kindred branches of knowledge. The appointment of Mr. Wallis also is a very judicious one. lie was one of the most valuable and active officers employed at Ilyde-parkin 1851, and, apart altogether from his acquirements as a teacher of the first principles of practical art, he has a rare and extensive acquaintance

with the merits of textile fabrics in every branch of their manufacture. Perhaps, however, for the material interests of this country, so far as they are likely to be effected by the New York Exhibition, the most valuable member of the new Commission is Mr. Whitworth, the leaded " Manchester tools." Mr. Whitworth ing maker in this country of what are callis the very best man that could he selected to concentrate into a report the mechanical results of the New York Exhibition ; and, ingenious and inventive as the Americans undoubtedly are, we need not be ashamed to send over to them, as a reporter, the mechanic who can, by the unaided exercise of his craft, measure the millionth part of an inch. The Commission goes to America carrying with it souvenirs of the display of 1851, with which all its members have been intimately associated. It is accredited neither to the Committee of the New York Exhibition nor to tbe Government, for the former is a private commercial body which this country could not officially acknowledge, and the latter only indirectly patronises the undertaking. It has, however, ample powers and a useful and dignified mission. It is charged with the duty of representing the industrial interests of England at the forthcoming display, and of reporting, in an authoritative manner, upon the results thereof. The Government have issued it upon the suggestion of the Surplus Commissioners, and they have further shown their zeal in the matter by getting several of the chief

departments of the state to contribute. The Ordnance, the Admiralty, the Mint, and the Board of Trade, through its School of Mines, intend to send articles for exhibition; and it is worthy of remark that, little as we may show, compared with the constituted authorities of other European communities, we have done far more as a body politic for the New York Exhibition than we did for our own. In Hyde-park the Government showed itself chiefly active in snubbing the ltoyal Commission and worrying it through Lord Seymour. Dr. Iloyle is busily engaged in selecting, on the part of the East India Company,

a brilliant show of Oriental manufactures wherewith to dazzle the Western world. About 800 British exhibitors, comprising the leading houses in important departments of our national industry, have sent contributions. Our artists arc admitted also to the field of competition which embraces paintings, and among the champions of the national industry is included the name of the Duke of Buecleugh. Considering the extent to which other European states as well as our own intend supporting the approaching Exhibition, it is a matter of some surprise that the building in which the display takes place is one of such small dimensions. The site upon which it stands is not more than 500 feet square, and the structure itself has been already supplemented by additions for machinery. We Londoners grumble at the want of space available for such objects, and the surplus of the late Exhibition has been sunk into one lump sum to secure more elbow-room for our public institutions; but in new York, with a Continent in the back ground, the evil seems to be still more severely felt, and they appear there to have been driven into a situation not much more convenient than that at one time contemplated for the display of 1851, when it was seriously proposed to hold it in Leicester-square. Only one-third of the area has been reserved for native exhibitors, the rest being devoted to the products of European industry and art. The opening is postponed till the first of June.

Is it not a " little curious" that II arhiet Martineau, an old maid, a "benign cerulean of the second sex," as Lord Byron calls her class, who " never loved," or if she did, yet who, if published accounts are true, shrunk from the nuptial bonds, and left her affianced lord in the lurch at the last moment þÿ is it not a little curious, we say, that such a woman should have written so exquisite a picture of true love as that which ensues? We once heard a distinguished American author remark, sitting by his " Dutchman's Fireside," that he kept for days out of the literary lady-traveller's way when she was trying to meet him. " There she was," said he, " going about with that long India-rubber ear-trumpet of hers, taking in every thing that was offered to it, just like an elephant going round with his trunk, drawing in here an apple, there a piece of cake, now a handful of nuts, and next, perhaps, a chew of tobacco. I wasn't going to contribute to her trunk, nor to the lining any others, when she had got home and printed her notes!" If the authoress, however, had met this unwilling host, and had told this " tale of love," doubtless he would have listened in " mute admiration." But we are forgetting the passage: "There is no other such crisis in human life as the crisis of Lovf.. The philosopher may experience uncontrollable agitation in verifying his principle of balancing systems of worlds, feeling perhaps as if he actually saw the creative hand in the act of sending the

planets forth on their everlasting way ; hut be knows at such a moment no emotions so divine as those of the spirit becoming conscious that it is beloved : be it the peasant-girl in the meadow, or the daughter of the sage, or the artisan beside his loom, or the man of letters musing by his fire-side. The warrior about to strike the decisive blow for the liberties of a nation is not in a state of such lofty resolution as those who, by joining hearts, are laying their joint hands on the whole wide realm of futurity for their own. The statesman, in the moment of success, is not conscious of so holy and so intimate a thankfulness as

they who are aware that their redemption has come in the presence of a new and sovereign affection. And these are many: they are in all corners of every land. The statesman is the leader of a nation ; the warrior is the grace of an age; the philosopher is the birth of a thousand years; hut the þÿLover where is he not f Wherever parents look round upon their children, there he has been: wherever children are at play together there he soon trill he; wherever there are roofs under which men dwell, wherever there is an atmosphere vibrating with human voices, there is the lover, and there is his lofty worship going onunspeakable, perchance, but revealed in the brightness of the eye, the majesty ot the presence, and the high temper ol the discourse. Men have been ungrateful and perverse, they have done what they could to counteract it, to debate this most heavenly influence of their life ; but the laws of their Maker are too strong, the benignity of their Father is too patient and fervent, for their opposition to withstand : and true love continues, and will continue, to send up its homage amidst the meditations of every eventide, and the busy hum of noon, and the song of the morning stars." þÿ Harper's Magazine.

A ncfilotc ol' W i>h cs. Tin; wolf resembles the dog in shape, but is generally larger and more muscular, as well as more savage in appearance. The leading peculiarity of the wolf, wherever it may be found, is ferocity of disposition, accompanied with a certain decree of meanness or cowardliness, which is toreigu to the character of the dog in all its varieties. It has been usual with naturalists to represent the wolf as lint metafile, or at least unsusceptible ol attachment to man. I bit this is now discovered t o be incorrect. The wild ferocious character of the wolf, it appears, is very much the result of the circumstances in which it is placed. Cuvier mentions the case of a young wolf which was brought up like a dog by a gentleman in France, and became familiar with every person whom it was in the habit of seeing ; learned to follow like a dog, was obedient, and attached to its master in an extreme degree. This remarkable case of the taming of a wolf is given as an instance of how much may be accomplished by early culture and kindness on even the wildest and most rapacious of animals. "Wolves wore at one time plentiful in Britain and Ireland, but it is long since they were extirpated. They still abound in the northern parts of Europe, particularly in ltussia, and are numerous in some parts ofFrance, where they commit dreadful devastations. They are likewise common in North America, where they are black in colour, and in some instances white. In the year 1704, a wolf committed the most dreadful

devastations in sonic particular districts ot Langucdoc, in the south of France, and soon became the terror of the whole country. According to the accounts given in the Paris gazette, it was known to have killed twenty persons, chiefly women and children; and public prayers are said to have been offered up for its destruction. It seems rather strange, that wolves were not yet banished from the thickly inhabited parts of France at the period to which wo refer. This is apparent from the following anecdote, which we þÿ quote from a London newspaper of 1838 : ' The winter before last, Monsieur do II , an advocate of Dijon, was returning rather late from shooting near that town, when his dog, a small pointer, which was a few paces in advance, ran suddenly back in evident alarm. The spot was a long hollow, formed by two sand-banks ; and as far as his eye could reach, ho could discover no cause for the animal's sudden terror, which sent him crouching to his feet, lie proceeded cautiously, however, cocking both barrels of his gun ; but for upwards of 200 yards, no cause of alarm presented itself. Indeed, he had forgotten the circumstance, and rested the gun across his shoulder, when the dog again sprang behind him with an affrighted yell. A wolf stood on the sand-bank, about thirty yards before him. Armed only with partridge-shot, Monsieur de B considered it most prudent to retreat, and gain a cross-road in the rear. to lie turned many yards, when, his horror and had not reastonishment, ho beheld another wolf barring his

path on that side. Neither as yet ventured to attack him, and as ho advanced, each retired ; but the other would draw closer to his heels. His situation became critical, for night was approaching, and he feared that with it more assailants would be down upon him ; and to this they both howled, as if to call a reinforcement, and the sportsman at length felt certain they were answered from the hills. No time was to be lost ; he rapidly advanced on one, and within twenty paces fired both barrels at him. The wolf fell wounded, and the other cleared the bank, evidently scared. Monsieur de B , following his example, took to his heels, and never drew breath till he had entered Dijon. On examining the snow next morning, it was ascertained that he had been liotly pursued to the very gates. As for the wounded wolf, a few bones were all that his comrades had left of him.' The following account of the rapacity of wolves in Ilussia, is given by a traveller, but of whose name we arc ignorant, from the manner it has come under our notice : þÿ ' A peasant, when one day in his sledge, was pursued by eleven of those ferocious animals : at this time lie was only about two miles from home, towards which lie urged his horse at the very top of his speed. At the entrance to his residence was a gate, which happened to be closed at the time ; but the horse dashed this open, and thus himself and his master found refuge within the courtyard. They were followed, however, by nine out of the eleven wolves ; but, very fortu-

nately, at the instant these had entered the enclosure, the gate swung back on its hinges, and thus they were caught as in a trap. From being the most ferocious of animals, the nature of these beasts, now that they found escape impossible, became completely changed : so far, indeed, from

AfliS, offering molestation to any one, they slunk into holes and corners, and allowed themselves to be slaughtered almost without making resistance.' The following singular adventure of General Putnam with a wolf, in the state of Connecticut, in North America, has been already made known in works of natural history, but may here appropriately be repeated : þÿ 'Some time after Mr. Putnam had removed to Connecticut, the wolves, which were then verynumerous, broke into his shecpfold, and killed seventy fine sheep and goats, besides worrying several lambs and kids. This dreadful havoc was committed by a she-wolf, which, with her annual whelps, had for several years infested the neighbourhood. The whelps were commonly destroyed by the vigilance of the hunters, but the old one was too sagacious to come within reach of gunshot ; and upon being closely pursued, she would generally fly to the western woods, and return the next winter with another litter of whelps. ' This animal at length became such an intolerable nuisance, that Mr. Putnam and five of his neighbours agreed to hunt alternately, in until they could destroy her, and two of them rotation, were to be constantly in pursuit. It was known that, having lost the toes from one foot by a steeltrap, she made one track shorter than the other. By this vestige the pursuers recognised, in a light snow, the route ol' the wolf. Having followed her to Connecticut river, and found she had turned back toward Poinfrct, they immediately return-

ed, and by ten o'clock next morning the blondhounds had driven her into a cave about three miles distant from Mr. Putnam's house. The people soon assembled with dogs, guns, straw, fire, and sulphur, to attack their common enemy, and several attempts were made to dislodge her from the den ; but the hounds came back wounded and intimidated, and neither the smoke of blazing straw, nor the fumes of brimstone, could compel her to ipiit her retirement. ' Wcariei 1 with these fruitless attempts, which had continued nearly twelve hours, Mr. Putnam proposed to his negro servant to go down into the cavern and shoot the wolf; and on his declining the hazardous service, the general resolved himself to destroy the ferocious animal, lest she should escape through sonic unknown fissure of the rock. Accordingly, having provided himself with several strips ol birch-bark, to light him in this darksome cave, he pulled off his coat and waistcoat-, and having a long rone fastened round his body, by which he might be drawn back at a concerted signal, he entered head foremost, with the blazing torch in his hand. ' The aperture of the cave, on the east side of a high ledge of rocks, is about two feet square : from thence it descends obliquely fifteen feet, and then running horizontally about ten more, it ascends sixteen feet towards its termination. The sides of this cavity consist of smooth solid rocks, which seem to have been divided from each other by an earthquake. The the top and bottom are also

being covered with ice, composed oi stone, and is entrance, in winter, extremely slippery. It is ill no place high enough for a man to raise himself upright, nor in any part more than three feet broad. ' Mr. Putnam having groped his passage to the horizontal part of the cavern, the most terrifying darkness appeared in front of the dim circle of light afforded by his torch, and all was silent on- as the house of death. Cautiously proceeding ward, he came to the ascent, which he slowly mounted on his hands and knees, till he discovered the glaring eye-balls of the welt, which was the sight of fire, she gnashed sitting at the extremity of the her den. Startled teeth, and gave, at a sullen growl, upon which the general kicked the rope, as a signal for pulling him out. The growling of the wolf, people at the mouth and of the cave hearing the imagining their friend to be in the most imminent danger, drew him out with such celerity, that his shirt was stripped over his head, and his skin severely lacerated. However, he boldly persisted in his resolution, and having adjusted his clothes, and loaded his gun with buck-shot, he descended a second time. On his second approach, the wolf assumed a very fierce and terrible countenance, howling, rolling her eyes, snapping her teeth, and dropping her head between her legs; but when she was on the very point of springing on him, Mr. l'utman fired at her head, and was immediately drawn out of the cave. After refreshing himself, and permitting the smoke to dissipate, he went down again,

and on applying his torch to the animal's nose, found her dead; then taking hold of her ears, and kicking the rope, he drew her forth, to the astonishment of all the spectators.' þÿ C /iambics s Miscellany.

AUSTRALIA. Papers from Perth, Western Australia, have been received to the 15th of January. The periodical meeting of the Western Australian Hank had just taken place, and the dividend declared was at t he rate of 12| per cent per annum. The harvest in the interior was nearly concluded, and the result was considered favourable; but some little difficulty had been experienced in obtaining labour, owing to the prevalence of influenza. Coal shale had been discovered in the neighbourhood of the Preston river, and also a new pastoral district to the eastward, the capabilities of which were regarded as important. Accounts from Sydney to the 15th of January have been received via Panama. The news from the diggings is on the whole favourable. The production of gold is said to be increasing. Trade was generally good and remunerative. The difficulties with respect to vessels getting away had apparently diminished. 1'ive vessels had sailed, having on board an aggregate of 00,837 ounces of gold ; and about a dozen others were announced to sail in the course of January and February. Much excitement had been caused by the discovery that spurious gold had been manufactured and sold to an enormous amount. It is stated that .£100,000 had been made in live months by the operators in this gold fraud. Some ot the persons had been apprehended, and one of them, a man named Carey, committed for trial. Further advices from Sydney to the 31st ot January have been received by the Yimiera. The Melbourne steamer

had not arrived. The yield of gold was unaltered. Several new fields had been discovered. The Times correspondent gleans from'pri vate intelligence that one ot them, on the confines of New South \\ ales, is likely to proven second Mount Alexander. Twenty- three cargoes from F.uropean and F.astern ports have changed hands at Sydney, and gone into consumption, since the beginning of the year, without material alteration in prices. The whole of the wool clip had been got in, but great delay took place in bringing it to market. High prices were ruling for both wool and tallow. Exchange had improved. The banks were selling at 4 per cent, and buying at 5A per cent, discount. Gold dust, was selling at 73s. to 74s. 3d. for Victoria ; the New South Wales dust at 2s. per ounce lower. Freights unaltered, hut more easily ' obtained. Money very plentiful. Arrived front Liverpool since 28th December: Eliza, Mary, Catharine, and lleejapore. The following fact, very strikingly illustrative of the expensi veness of living at Melbourne, has been communicated to us by a friend. A young man left this city last season for Australia. He spent the greater part of the summer at the diggings, but on thcnpproach of the rainy

season, having had no previous experience ot roughing it in the bush, he judged it prudent to betake himself to a locality where he could have a roofover his head. He accordingly returned to Melbourne, designing to remain there till the return of spring. On experiencing, however, the rate of living at Melbourne, he, like a canny Scotchman, set himself down to calculate whether he

A IIkiii Price for a Kiss. þÿ A very good story is told ot' an acquaintance of ours, a commercial traveller, who was passing through the county Monaghan some short time since, lie took up his quarters, it seems, at a certain hotel, and having comforted his inner man with a good dinner, a steaming " full flowing bowl," and some of those other good things a hotel can always afford, he was become right merry, and a young lady, connected with the establishment, happening to come into the room in which lie was, nothing would satisfy our gentleman but a kiss. As he was rather a well-faced young fellow and respectable, the fair one was not very loath ; modesty, however, would not permit her to give it without a slight struggle. In this struggle a drawer containing a number of china articles was pulled out to the floor, and the contents shattered " Oh dear ! see what I've done" from to fragments. The accident elicited an the gallant, and a response of " No harm done" from the young lady, and so the matter dropped at that time. We cannot state positively that he received the kiss ; however, judging of others by oneself, and considering there was no serious disinclination on her part, we may take it for granted that he did obtain it. On glueing his eyes along the several items of the bill presented next morning, how must he have stared on discovering "for china broken þÿ five pounds!" lie demurred, but in the end paid. Just at that instant, the mischievous fair one thrust in her head, and
asked him if lie would have a kiss. Bowing low and politely, he declined it at the price. þÿ Armagh Guardian.

Launch of the Largest Steamer in the Wori.I). þÿ On Tuesday last the Atrato, belonging to the Royal West India Mail Steam-packet Company, "the largest vessel that ever slid down the ways since the world began," was launched from the yard of Messrs. Caird and Co., at Greenock. She is all iron, and has been built to supply the place of the unfortunate Demerara in the squadron of the Royal Mail Company. Shading the Eves. þÿ Some people cover their eyes with green or other shades when anything is the matter with them. This is wrong. It is now ascertained by the best oculists that shades injure the sight instead of strengthening it, from their creating beat and inflammation in the parts affected. If the eye be injured, and light insupportable, the best way is to tie a cool linen handkerchief over it. þÿ Cheerful V isitor.

The crew of the screw-steamer Calcutta, now lying in the Southampton Dock, and which brought home the last Mauritius and Cape Mail, are nearly all blacks. There are nearly eighty of them, consisting of Lascars, Arabs, and Negroes. What a unique and meaning expression was that of' a young Irish girl, in giving testimony against an individual in a court of justice the other day. " Ar- rali, sir," said she, " I'm sure he never made his mother smile." There is a biography of unkiudness in that short and simple sentence.

We had had a fine passage, and were looking forward to the end of our voyage in about a week. I was the only passenger, and of course was thrown in a great measure on my own resources for amusement, the chief of which was testing the powers of an admirable glass of London manufacture upon every vessel that shewed itself above the horizon. Air. Ilcet'hcr Stoivc in tlngiaiid. Many people will observe with regret that Mrs. Stowe's stay in this country will be very short. The crowils that awaited her at every station on her journey from Liverpool to Glasgow show how great is the desire to obtain a mere sight of her. This is natural enough ; but we had hoped that when the staring was over and the first eagerness of welcome past, we should be able to obtain, m peace and quiet, from one who knows so much, some information which may be useful for practical guidance. The occasion of a service like hers is too great and too serious to be disposed of with compliments and empty enthusiasm on the one hand, and recrimination and vituperation on the other. A book written for the relief of an oppressed heart, and going out to stir the hearts of whole nations, is no theme for flattery, or occasion for such spiritual pastime as the most ordinary of our May meetings are expected to yield ; and it is worse still to fall into taunting and bickering about national faults and misfortunes. Having got Mrs. Stowc among us, we hoped to keep her and her busband long enough to learn a great deal from them of what must be under the surface, and all round about the subject-matter of " Uncle Tom's Cabin." Hut they say they must make haste home, and be" bard at work again in the United States by the 1st of June. This is an instance of American rapidity which we would gladly have spared ; but we must be all the more diligent to learn what we can during the month of

their stay, which will afford, no doubt, a series of public addresses, more or less like that of Glasgow. From this lirst address we derive one fact, which it is of the highest importance that we should consider. Professor Stowe agrees with all other authorities in sayport ing that sugar and rice would that American slavery ; and not sup- if it depended on those products, it would die in a year. No Hritish traveller in the United States can have any doubt of this. He could almost count the estates on the low-lying lands which grow rice; and he observes that, cruel as is the aspect of slavery in the sugar-growing districts, they are narrowly circumscribed: so that the United States have to import sugar largely for their own congrievance. sumption. And that the toil is great Hcsides tobacco is no light, in comparison with that of sugar and cotton-growing, the consumption of tobacco, vast as it is, can never support slaves by millions. It is the cotton that is the vantage ground of slavery. So Professor Stowe tells us; and so we have often been told before; and we always like to hear it, we see a if this be true, that because way we think, out of the evil. Professor Stowe was reminded of cotton from the hour when he landed in Liverpool to that in which he addressed the citizens of Glasgow. "In this country," said he, "is the great market for American cotton; and it is cotton which sustains American slavery. I do not say you can do without it. I wish I could do without it myself. I

have a large family to clothe ; I am a poor man ; and I must use cotton ; but I wish 1 could do without it. Hut the thing is, can we live without supporting American slavery ?" That is a question to which thousands now feel no hesitation in answering þÿ Yes, we can live without supporting American slavery, and without depriving ourselves of cotton either. If that were the alternative, we should not say a word; because we certainly could not wish to deprive millions of our people of the healthful, cheap, and convenient

S '£ Q & <© 1 ii T I 3. clothing that our cotton manufacture affords, or the millions of the maintenance they derive from our manufacture and commerce in that article. In short, it would be nonsense to think of it, and mere cant to talk of it, as the American planters and Hritish manufacturers know perfectly well. Hut we know something else which may be less familiar to Prolessor Stowe than to bis anti-slavery friends in this country; that cotton maybe had, whenever we exert ourselves properly to world parts of the get it, from many other than the United States. When we began seriously to see what was doing in India in the way of cotton easy growing, the Carolina saw ; but when they planters grew un- what the difficulties were of bringing the produce down the ghats how many bullocks þÿ were lost, and how many bales were lost, and how many bales were spoiled the by mud and dust, they in laughed. effect of railroads India has Hut yet to be tried, together with that of a good many more ameliorations which we may hope for, from our strengthening determination to obtain better government for India. Then there is Australia. Hefore the gold was discovered, there seemed some reason to believe that our Australian colonies might become a chief cotton field of Great Hritain ; and we do not see that the discovery ot the gold need spoil the prospect altogether, though it may cause some delay in the realisation. If labourers flock into Australia in sufficient numbers we may have bulk of Australian cotton yet. tine of

the oldest cotton brokers in Liverpool, since dead þÿ a man who had grown cotton himself in the United States in his early days þÿ declared, in 1H-1S, after examining divers specimens of Australian cotton, that that product would make a great country hereafter of that distant dependency of ours. So lately as last summer, Mr. Hazley, the President ol the Manchester Ch niber of Commerce, declared "his opinion that such superior and excellent attributes of perfect cotton have been rarely seen in Manchester; and that the samples offered indisputably prove most tralia to produce the capability ol Aus- useful and beautiful cotton, adapted to the Hnglisli markets." Then, again, there arc the West Indies. In Jamaica, specimens of very fine cotton are seen, in the midst of the desolation and dreary waste of that island, where there are millions of' acres of fertile land, of which only half a million have ever been appropriated, and where there is no regular traflic, or means of conveyance by land or water, except fifteen miles of railroad. There may be a fine commerce in sugar between Jamaica and this country yet, after all that is come and gone, and we hope there will be; but there will still be hundreds of thousands ol acres to spare for cotton ; and cotton is a product which it may suit the convenience of the coloured people extremely well to give their attention to when they increase in numbers. This is proved by the success of whatever experiments have been made in Africa; and experiments have

been tried there of a very important kind. As long as it was merely a suggestion of the Missionaries, in their eagerness to divert the natives from slave trading, and to furnish them with resources which might raise their condition, men of business might be excused from attending seriously to proposals of a cotton trade. They might be expected to smile and shake their heads, and say that a vast deal depends on the ginning, packing, Ac., ot cotton, if the soil and the plant were ever so good. Hut Manchester itself now avows that great results may be anticipated from the humble efforts ot the mission-

aries and their friends. The quality o the samples sent home would be excel" lent if the cleaning were well managed : and the increase of the quantity grown is so encouraging, that the cleaning is to be well managed. Machinery and men are sent out, not merely to instruct the natives, but to conduct the business, which has become by far too great for the strengt h and time oftlie missionaries. A stronger evidence even than this is the presence of those vigilant and ubiquitous nurses of commerce, the Americans, in the central parts of Africa, soliciting the cotton growth, as if they had none at home. They are present at all commercial births ; and they have an instinct which leads them to the right spot in the nick of time ; and their alighting in the centre of Africa, stimulating the production of cotton, shows that the season for the production of African cotton has come. Silently, stealthily, they have gone up the great rivers from the west : and there, in the heart of the continent, are they lighted upon by travellers from the north. As we derive one kind of lesson from encountering a Russian fort in all the out-skirts of the world, so we may derive another kind of lesson from stumbling upon an American factory, virtual or visible in all the centres of the inhabited world ; and if we find our cousins fingering cotton, we may take the hint, and may at an early day cease to be dependent upon them for the staple of our chief manufacture. There are many inducements to an independence

which we have not yet contemplated with a sufficient seriousness. It is not for our dignity, it is not for our safety, it is not for our moral welfare, to be absolutely dependent on any one conntry, in any one respect, for a supply of a necessary of life, when that necessary may be had from so many different places. It is not pleasant to know that the old Liverpool broker avowed that lie dared not say publicly what he thought of Australian cotton, lest he should lose all his American business. It is not pleasant to bear from Professor Stowe that the price of a slave, who was formerly worth ItMt dollars, has risen, through our demand for cotton, to £300. It is not pleasant to think that the moral sense and judgment of any portion ol' our countrymen arc under coercion by commercial interests. The one pleasant thing about the whole affair is the certainty that, if cotton be all, we can get out of the difficulty. We can penetrate Western Africa for geographical purposes: we can ascend the Nile for antiquarian recreation : we can go to India to make war, and to Australia for gold, and to China for tea and silk, and to the Pacific Islands to Christianise the people: þÿ therefore we can go to these same places tor cotton, whenever we so will. And we shall trill it when we see fully, clearly, and universally that this is the one way in which, without offence or mischief, we can bear our share iu the extinction of remaining negro slavery, and save our national peace and com-
mercial independence from a certain dcrrec of peril. þÿ Ihii/y News.

After a residence of two years, the Reverend Gentleman is i compelled for to the undertake a voyage Europe, especial purpose of re- to ' establishing his health, seriously impaired by the debilitating effects of a tropical climate, as well as too arduous and zealous application to his ministerial duties. tion that such absence will be only temporary, confirmed by the repeated assurances of the Minister, whose intended departure is a source of general regret. It is highly grateful to allude to a public demonstration, evincing the tribute due to an individual who has accomplished a faithful mission ; on this occasion the subject is of peculiar interest in a moral point of view, and we derive infinite satisfaction whilst recording that tribute to express our best wishes for the speedy return of the Reverend J. Pratt, to re-assume the Ministry of the Roman Catholic Church in this Island. Meanwhile, the functions of cure of this parish will devolve on the Reverend Michki. From Chambers's Miscellany. Secnc with a Pirate. ( Coucludod. ) Now, I had never seriously considered the probability that I might also be killed in an approaching melee, for I thought that the captain intended to throw open his ports and shew his sham guns, and at that, of course, the schooner would take fright. But when he began to talk about death in such a serious strain, I began to feel very uncomfortable ; and not being naturally a warrior, I wished myself anywhere else than on board the Patrick Henry. There I was, however, without a chance of escape ; and I suggested to the captain, that it would be as well for me to put a letter into the bottle also, in case of any accident to both of us, which was agreed to ; and wo arranged that if either survived, and had the opportunity, the letter of the unfortunate should be safely forwarded to its destination. After this little piece of preparation, the captain took me by the hand. ' 'Tis well,' said he ; are you ' willing to share with mc the post of danger ? Do not suppose I am unaccustomed to the perils of a sea-fight : no, young man ; I've supported the glory of the thirteen stripes in many a gallant action, and have witnessed the death of those honoured and esteemed as the sons of liberty. Y ct they were fighting for their country, and it was their duty to hold their lives cheap ; but you are a passenger, and should be under my protection þÿ yet I ask you to share my danger. I wish some one to stand by me on the platform, and help me to manage the swivel. Hands are scarce,

and I don't know where else to place you.' The hardy fellow's eyes glistened as he made the pro- ' posal, to which I of course instantly agreed. Thankee, thankee,' he replied, and relapsed into his former character. 'Twas strange ; he had always appeared on board his vessel as a common Yankee captain, with little to say, and with a rough uncouth manner but little removed from his men. Yet he at once, though evidently inadvertently, assumed the air and manner of a polished gentleman ; and it certainly struck ine that the latter character appeared more natural to him than the former. There was evidently a mystery about him, and I determined to find it out when more opportune circumstances should occur. We went on deck, and the men were still hanging about waiting for the orders of their captain to make them start. These were soon given. The cooper and the carpenter were ordered to bring up all hatchets, and other offensive and defensive weapons, and with the muskets and rifle they were distributed among the crew, who received their orders to use them in repelling any attempt to board. The schooner had now come down within half a mile of us, when she suddenly took down her square-sail, and hauled her wind, to have a look at us. I daresay she did not know what to make of our seeming indifference. Presently a cloud of smoke burst from her side, and a ball came skip- ping over the water, and passed astern of us. ' I thought so,' said the captain ; ' now, lads, shew her our stripes.' A ball of bunting flew up to

the end of our mizen-peak, rested an instant, and fluttered out into the American ensign. The smoke drifted away from the schooner, and she ran up at her gaff the ensign of the Columbian Republic. ' That's 'tcrnally the way with them blackguards ; they are always making a fool of some republic. Scarcely were the words out of his mouth, when another column of smoke burst from the schooner, and another ball came skip þÿ skipping along towards us, but, catching a ' swell, it plunged in, and we saw no more of it. That fellow now, I take it, is a good shot, so we'll not wait for another. Clue up the main-sail, boys ; haul aft the weather main-braces ; clue up the foresail ; luff her, man, luff her a little moreþÿ steady,' burst from our captain's mouth ; the orders were obeyed with the quickness of a well-disciplined crew, and our ship was hove to. ' Now, my lads, take your stations, four to each port, on the weather-side, but do nothin' till I tell ye.' The men took their stations, as directed, round each log on the weather-side, and I followed the captain to the platform where our carronade was mounted. It was loaded to the muzzle with bits of iron, musket-balls, lumps of lead, and various other missiles, for the captain had conjectured truly þÿ there were no balls on board The schooner hove to, and a boat was lowered, and crowded with men. It approached rapidly, pulled by eight rowers. The muzzle of our carronadc was depressed as much as possible, and made to bear on the water about fifty yards
from the ship. The captain stood with his speaking-trumpet in one hand, and a handspike, with which he shifted the position of the gun as re-

3 T» <8 UJ It a Hi ji. T It 3» quired, in the other. The schooner's boat approached, coolly,' said the captain in an undcr-tone. Boy, ' Now, and sir, keep steady, and obey my ' orders was pulling rapidly to get alongside. fetch the iron that's heating in the galley þÿ run.' The boy ran, and returned with the iron rod heated at one end, which was handed to me. ' When I tell you fire, fire, as you value your life and those on board.' The captain now put his speaking-trumpet to his mouth, and hailed the boat, which was within a hundred yards of us. ' Stop þÿ no nearer, or I'll blow you all out of the waterþÿ keep off, keep off, or, I say, I'll' At that instant the man at the bows of the boat, who appeared to take the command, gave an order, and a volley from several muskets was fired at us. I heard the balls hit about me, and turned to look for the captain, to receive my order to fire. He was on his knee behind the cannon, and holding it by the breech. ' Why, captain ! what's the matter ? are you hit ?' He rallied. 'Nothing þÿ they're coming.' He gave another barrel þÿ hoist to the gun, cast his eye hurriedly along its ' Fire , and be quick !' I needed not a second bidding, for the boat was close alongside. The smoke burst from the txueh-hole with a hiss, and for an instant I thought the gun had missed fire, but in the next it exploded with dous report, that deafened me. ' Throw open a tremenyour ports, boys, and shew them your teeth,' roared the captain through his trumpet, and his voice sounded hideously unnatural. In an in-

stant every port was up, and our gnus protruded their muzzles. I had fancied that I heard a crash, followed by wild screams, immediately upon the discharge of the cannon ; but the report had deafened me, and the smoke, which was driven back in my face, had so shrouded me, that I could not see ; the unearthly shout of the captain had also for the moment driven the idea from my my mind, and I now grasped my gun to repel boarders. But my hearing had not deceived me ; for, as the smoke was borne away to leeward, the whole scene of destruction burst upon my sight. The cannon had been most truly pointed, and its contents had shivered the hapless boat, killing or wounding almost every person in her. The longest lifetime will hardly efface that scene from my mind. The stern of the boat had been carried completely away, and it was sinking by the weight of the human beings that clung to it. As it gradually disappeared, the miserable wretches struggled forward to the bows, ami with horrid screams and imprecations battled for a moment for what little support it might yield. The dead and the dying were floating and splashing around them, while a deep crimson tinge marked how fatal had been that discharge. ltopes were thrown over, and everything done to save those that were not destroyed by the cannon shot, but only three þÿ were saved the greater part went down with the out of the boat's crew of twenty-four boat to which they clung. The whole scene of destruction did not last ten minutes, and all was again quiet. The bodies of

those who had been shot did not sink, but were driven by the wind and sea against the side of the ship. From some the blood was gently oozing, and floating around them ; others, stiff in the convulsion in which they had died, were grinning or frowning with horrible expression. One body, strong and muscular, with neat white trousers, .and a leathern girdle in which were stuck two pistols, floated by, but the face was gone ; some merciless ball had so disfigured him, that all trace of human expression was destroyed. He was the pirate captain. But where was the schooner ? She lay for a few minutes after the destruction of her boat ; and whether alarmed at our appearance, or horrified at the loss of so many of her men, I know not, but she slipped her foresail, and stood away as close to the wind as possible. We saw no more of her. The excitement of the scenes we had just passed through, prevented our missing the captain ; but so soon as the schooner bore away, all naturally expected his voice to give some order for getting again under-way. But no order came. Where was he ? The musket discharge from the boat, with the unearthly voice that conveyed the orders for the ports to be thrown open, flashed across my mind. I ran to the platform. The captain was there, lying on his face beside the gun that he had pointed with such deadly effect. He still grasped the speaking-trumpet in his hand, and I shuddered as I beheld its mouthpiece covered with blood. ' The captain's killed !' I cried, and stooped
to raise him. ' I believe I am,' said he ; ' take mc to the cabin.' A dozen ready hands were stretched to receive him, and he was taken below, and carefully laid

on a sofa. ' Ay,' he said, ' I heard the crash ; my ear knows too well the crash of shot against a plank to be mistaken, and my eye has pointed too many guns to miss its mark easily now. But, tell me, is any one else hurt ?' 'No, thank God,' I said; 'and I lioyc you are not so badly hit.' ' Bad enough. But cut open my waistcoat þÿ 'tis here.' A mouthful of blood stopped his utterance, but he pointed to his right side. I wiped his mouth, and we cut off his waistcoat as gently as possible. There was no blood ; but on removing his shirt, we discovered, about three inches on the right of the pit of the stomach, a discoloured spot, about the size of half-a-crown, darkening towards its centre, where there was a small wound. A musket ball had struck him, and from there being no outward bleeding, I feared the worst. We dressed the wound as well as circumstances would permit ; but externally it was trifling þÿ the fatal wound was within. The unfortunate sufferer motioned for all to leave him but me ; and calling me to his side : ' I feel,' said he, 'that! am dying; the letter, promise me that you will get it forwarded þÿ 'tis to my poor widow. Well, I've tempted this death often, and escaped, and 'tis hard to be struck by a villain's hand. But God's will be done.' I promised that I would personally deliver the letdying man ; ' you will then see my Helen and from Curagoa. ' Thank you truly,' said the ter, for that I intended returning to New York my child, and can tell them that their unfortu-

nate husband and father died thinking of them This ship and cargo are mine, and will belong to my family. Stranger, 1 was not always what 1 now seem. But I could not bear that the Yankee skipper should be kuown as he who once.' A sudden flow of blood prevented his finishing the sentence. I tried to relieve him by change of posture, but in vain ; he muttered some incoherent sentences, by which his mind seemed to dwell upon former scenes of battle for the republic, and of undeserved treatment. He rallied for one instant, and with a blessing for his family, and the name of Helen on his lips, he ceased to breathe. The body of our unfortunate captain, was next day committed to the waves amidst the tears of us all. Our voyage was prosecuted to an end without further interruption. 1 did not forget the wishes of the dying man : how faithfully I fulfilled them, and how I have been rewarded, or how satisfactory to mc was the previous history of the poor captain, need not to be told. Suffice it to say, that I am settled in Elm Cottage, Bloemendaal, and am the happiest son-in-law, husband, and father in the United States.

So many complaints have been made, and often with so very little or no cause, against the existing system ot Ocean Mail communication, that it is now known the British Government, as well as that of the United States, have resolved upon framing no additional Contracts, nor renewing those now in operation as their respective terms expire þÿ after which the old method will be resorted to of transmitting the mail bags by sailing packets, or such other chance opportunities as may offer; and then the advantages of steam communication will cease with most of the I Vest India Colonies ! ! In order, therefore, that the residents in the Colonies may be roused to some sense of the consequences involved and likely to result from the hostility they have heretofore so virulently manifested towards the mail packets, it may be well for us here to give publicity to the above facts, stubborn as they are, and will prove so to those who from a rash agitation have caused the aforesaid Governments to adopt so lirm a determination ! It will then be discovered that a few days occasional delay in the receipt of mails coming thousands of miles, and subject to so many contingencies of wind, weather, branch packet routes, <fcc., is really no substantial grievance after all, yet often so ridiculously magnified, that we can well understand how disgusted must be the Managers of the Packets, and the British Ministers, at hearing such paltry inconveniences set forth as ruination to the

Colonies! What shall we say when the sugar ship carries home her own advices ; and sucli will be the case, for the clamorous action of the West India Colonists against the present contract system must eventually cause the steam packets to be discontinued, and then it will be found, when too late, that steamers, and those of an uncertain speed, will run on a Trunk Line, and even on that only when they can get enough passengers and freight to defray expenses. our namesake of the London " Times," We have lately been sorry to notice forgetful of our motto þÿ " Truth and justice," attacking the West India Company so violently ; mis-statements being frequently made, and circumstances so distorted," that the reader is led to erroneous conclusions. If the Great "Times" has its own motives to serve by such attacks, we of the Little "Times" have the good of the West Indies so much at heart that we are emboldened to make the attempt to warn the good folks around us of the trap into which they are likely to be decoyed, namely, mail plan, þÿ the abolition of the present contract following another sort of " abolition the plain truth being that, ," the poor colonists will be left to shift for themselves as regards the conveyance of their mails. Situated as we are at the principal meeting ground of the Company's steamers in the West Indies, we could make up a lot of little grievances against them, but invariably we see sufficient cause to make allowances, and many are the 'ins'

and 'outs' associated with so gigantic an operation, which no human foresight can control. Let it always be borne in mind fhat we (in the Colonies) might be much worse off than we are ; and without a doubt we will be much worse off when it comes to pass that the ' contract system'' is exchanged for the 1 chance system:

8 <© <© SL ATI! 3 A few years ago the West India Company ran a line, without any Government allowance, between St. Thomas, Bermuda and New York, but it did not half pay its expenses ; and we know from good authority that the Clnahii screw steamer Merlin does not return here again, but that a sailing vessel will supply the line between Bermuda and St. Thomas for the present, and the line will most probably be discontinued altogether when the present term of the Government allowance ceases. The West India Company are also trying, at this moment, a line between Chagres, Jamaica and Savannah, without any subsidy from the British Government; but the carriage of passengers and mails on that route does not we are told, pay the cost of the coals consumed, although the ship is a very good one, and as we observed when she was in this port, on her way to take up that route, expressly fitted for the conveyance of first and second class passengers.

Although we have little or no fear that Saint Thomas will ever want steam communication with Europe, the United States, and America generally, for our geographical position will ensnrcitto us, still we would rather have it fixed, settled, and regular, even though not the most expeditious in preference to its being uncertain, and coming upon us in fits and starts. But many of the West India Colonies would he very differently served, in fact would seldom or never see a steamer, if the present contract system be abandoned.

We have been drawn into the foregoing remarks after perusing certain articles in some Scotch papers which have been politely lent us by a friend, relating to the recent launch of the magnificent Iron Ocean Steam-ship Atrato, for the West India Mail Service, respecting which vessel the 'Greenock Advertiser' states as follows : þÿ " The construction of such a ship as the Atrato, and the recent purchase of La l'lata, afford the strongest evidence of the earnest desire of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company to fulfil their engagements with the Government, and their duty to the public. Most unfortunate and distressing circumstances, over which the Directors had no control, thwarted and delayed the execution of their hold intentions and liberal expenditure. It is perhaps not to be wondered at that passengers delayed, while on missions of vital importance to them, and merchants anxious about bills and remittances, should occasionally grumble at disappointments on the arrival and despatch of mails ; but it must be borne in mind that delays caused, by circumstances which no body of men can control, will often occur in the course of a fortnightly service embracing twenty-eight separate ports, each with peculiarities of its own for retarding the landing and departure of mails and passengers, and we have no doubt the feeling against the Company will subside when the public come to see the enormous expenditure and the great anxiety incurred in order to conduct their work satisfactorily. Though dis-

posed to grumble, the community will not long continue to abuse men showing an evidently fair and reasonable desire to accommodate. The Company have now at work a fleet of nineteen ships, above 32,000 aggregate tonnage, propelled by 8770 horses' power of machinery, and they have in progress the Atrato, and other four vessels of 0000 tons in all, with above 2000 horses' power machinery þÿ making a total of above 42,000 tons, and 11,000 horses' power."

In the Money Article of the London "Times," of the 28lh ultimo, we read the following : þÿ "The views of the Government on the mail contract system expressed in the House of Lords last night have been received in the City with gratification. The improvidence of former Cabinets, which has saddled the country with annual payments amounting to 800,000/. a-year, is to be remedied upon every occasion when the falling in of contracts may afford an opportunity. In the case of the cancelled contract with the Australian Company, tenders are to be invited from new quarters for the performance of the bi-monthly service which has thus lapsed, but the sum to be granted is very small, and the contract is to be given to those who shall offer to perform the voyage in the shortest period, no dictation being exercised with regard to the route to be chosen, so that the advocates of the Panama line will be placed on a footing with competitors via the Cape or elsewhere. In discussing these points, all parties seemed ready to condemn the course hitherto pursued, although it was attempted to apologize for some of the early contracts by the plea that the vessels and stations for their fulfilment required an outlay which no company would have ventured upon in the absence ot' a lengthened grant, and that without such an arrangement there would have been no steam communication at all. The argument in this respect, however, apart from being inherently unsound, afforded no justificati on
of the recent renewal of the Curia rd and West India subsidies, the former at 171,304/., and the latter at '270,1100/. per annum."

I'd like to have you give me your candid opinion of it. A friend of mine luul the impudence to sav this morning that it was not an original ! I should like to hear another man say that it was not an original ! But you come and see it, and tell me honestly what you think of its authenticity." It strikes us very that a man would not be apt to give a " candid" opinion under those circumstances. This freedom of opinion is not unlike the liberty of action said to have been granted by Col. M'Lank to the troops under his command, before going into winter-quarters at Valley Forge. They were suffering for provisions and clothing, and Congress had been repeatedly petitioned for that relict which it was not in their power to hestow. Under this state of things, Colonel M'Lank paraded his band of suffering soldiers, and thus addressed then:: "Fellow-soldiers, you have served your country faithfully and truly. We've fought hard fights together against our common enemy. You are in a bad way for comfortable clothes, it is true, and it grieves my very heart to see you tracking your feet in blood on the frozen ground. But Congress can not help it, nor can General Washington or I. But if any of you wish to return home, yon can go. Let such of you as would like to go home step out four paces in front þÿ but the first man that steps out, if I don't shoot him
my name is not M'Lane." It is perhaps needless to add, that not a solitary "volunteer" homeward was to be found. þÿ 1 lar /ter's M ogazi ne.

From the St. Thomas Times, June I, 1853. THE COLONIAL BUDGET. nies was read a first time in the " Folke/hing," On the 13th April, the budget for these Colowhen the following interesting debate took place : Mr. A. F i. age rose and þÿsaid It will be remembered that when the finance-law was discussed here, no mention was, so to say, made of revenues or expenses of the W. I. Colonies, lie cause, as it was stated, a Report was expected from the Colonial Council, and from the Governor of said Islands. That is contained in the printed papers now before us, and it is with much satisfaction, no doubt, that we have received the first report sent over to us from that Council, and that we learn that the Colonies arc heard in their own concerns. 1 am of opinion that a satisfactory and advantageous relation between the Mother Country and the Colonics can only be obtained by gradually, anil as much as possible, Hearing to a Colonial half-government. It is by that means only they can develop their resources to advantage, and we be benefitted by our connexion with them. It is evident that it cannot be done at once, but I am sure an enlightened Government will see that by proposing that the Colonies should govern themselves, as far as practicable, we arc striking the proper course. Other Countries are forced to do the same, in order to keep the Mother Country and the Colonies together. It is well known what innumerable dissentions have occurred between the governing State and the Colonies ; that constant complaiuts have taken

place þÿ now that a Governor was too extravagant ; then that another one was too parsimonious ; again, that a Law issued at home was not fit for the Colony ; in short, disputes have arisen on all possible subjects, and it is clear that a distance of thousands of miles makes it exceedingly difficult to govern in detail. Hitherto we have been accustomed not to sec a balance ot revenues, but a surplus of expenditure for the Colonies ; in this law we have the first pleasant indication that we may perhaps in future get rid of expenses, however it may go with the revenue. I acknowledge that we have no great claim to have a direct income from the Colonies. Here is a budget shewing 9,452 Kbd. 29 Sk. less revenue than expense, which is comparatively a great improvement ; and from different indications in the law, we may expect next year to have no direct deficiency. I say direct, because the House will recollect that we have indirectly to pay for the Colonies, and which we for the present cannot well get rid of, in the shape of a reduced duty on their sugars, which is against us, in the amount of 100,000 to 125,000 Rbd. annually. That is a direct loss which we suffer from the Colonies, and which we must as yet suffer for some time. In stating this, 1 cannot abstain from mentioning that it would appear advisable to equalize the export duties on sugars at St. Croix, instead of demanding double duties, as far as I remember, on their being exported to foreign countries ; for even if we did not loose
one skilling per lb. Customs' duties here, it appears to me improper to prevent the Colonics

from exporting their sugars to foreign countries. I refer this matter to the consideration of Government, but I do not say that we should act withaut first asking the consent of the Colonial Council. I shall make a few observations with regard to some items of revenue and expenses, though expecting that a Committee will be appointed. Custom-house revenues (St. Croix) are put down at $ 110,000, but I find that on an average of the last three years they have been $ 98,000. Now, it appears very uncertain if the first sum will be attained, or the result be quite different, considering the chances connected with that source of revenue. Amongst the expenses, I find it proposed to increase the Governor's salary from $8,000 to $10,- 000; it was not expressly recommended, nor was it opposed by the Colonial Council, and it appears that the Governor has not interested himself further in the matter. As far as I know, the present Governor was sent to the West Indies on a promise to remain two years, at a salary of $8,000. In case he gives satisfaction, which 1 do not know, it would appear desirable to secure his services for a longer period, and it is perhaps proper to fix his salary and table money at $10,000, considering that he, without having an extravagant house, ought occasionally to see the public officers, and strangers coming to the Islands. I shall, therefore, not in the least object to leave that sum at $10,000. It is furthermore proposed to continue the expense of the Commandant of St. Thomas, though

all seem agreed that this office ought to be connected with that of the Government of St. Croix, þÿ it might perhaps, be proper, considering this change as likely to take place, to grant only one half of this item $4,500, for a half year, and employ the rest towards the Steamboat connexion, which 1 am immediately going to mention. The military expenses are here posted with $ 12,000 instead of $1 16,000, and I hope it may 1 be possible to save the $4000 formerly granted in addition. As far as 1 know, the garrisons consist in 400 men in all. A radical economy might be effected if a complete Police Force could he organized in the Islands always, provided that the Colonies are allowed to regulate matters themselves ; T think that so much economy would thereby be effected, that a future lludget would look quite different. The sum proposed for a Vessel-of-War amounts this time to only 29,700 Rbd., in consequence of the Colonies having protested against Laving a Brig stationed there for their un a account, and I think that they have had good reason to object to (laying that expense. 1 do not see clearly thai such a brig is of great defence or advantage to the Colonics; and T should think that if we now and then sent a Man-of-War to the Colonies, and at the same time to other ports of the American Continent, ijj-c., f. i. Rio Janeiro, and other important places, to show the Hag, we might almost effect the same with regard to the Colonies, and benefit the Danish commerce generally. We

might also thereby avoid loosing a great many of the crew in the sickly season, as the ease was this year. It is a very great part of the whole cost, which is put down at (10,000 Rbd. for a year, and it weighs heavily on such a small Budget. 1 shall merely refer the matter for the consideration of those better acquainted with the circumstances, and only add, that, it seems possi ble to do away with the Man-of-War, if we grant the sum proposed for having a Steamer between the Islands. It is quite clear that just as we require to have railroads in this Country, so those Islands require a constant communication by Steamers, to promote their trade and future development, more so, as such a communication has already been established between St. Thomas and Porto Rico. It is already observed that the Government might be centered in one place if a Steamer was stationed to run between St. Croix and St. Thomas, and it appears to me that when the Steamer was armed with one or two guns, it might be almost as useful as the Brig-of-War. There is a proposal from two respectable commercial houses, one at St. Thomas, and the other at St. Croix, to maintain a regular steam communication, provided a yearly sum were to be contributed towards the same. 1 should very much like that it were possible further to extend this, so as to bring the Islands in further communication with Porto Rico, which is so very important to St. Thomas. If the proposal is acceded to, the Colonies will have their Steamer running af-

ter about nine months, and if we could grant a further sum, the said two houses might perhaps stretch a point to bring it about sooner. The whole Budget is such that we cannot expect to sec it again in its present shape, as it is in contemplation to reform all the Judicial, Police, and Municipal Departments, and if the Colonies should

succeed in hitting the right points, and we allow them to do what is right, they are likely to save, for their own benefit, a good many expenses for salaries and other matters. It cannot be expected that we should make more than general remarks in a matter like this ; it will be clear to all that we cannot enter upon the details. There may be a few items which we may propose differently, but on the whole we are likely to confine ourselves to a general view of how matters stand. We will be obliged to leave it to the local Councils and to the Government to do what is best, and also on this account, I consider it highly desirable that the Colonies should gradually be brought to govern themselves. When that takes place, I shall no longer consider it as a mere wish, but as something to be expected, that the Colonies may provide for the sum now demanded from us. (To be continued.)

Tin \. Yoi k Journal of Ei.mnierre, Mm/ 1 <5. 1 The Crystal Palace. þÿ This week will make a great change in the appearance of the Crystal Palace. To-day or to-morrow, the large lantern, twenty feet in diameter, intended to surmount the dome, will be hoisted to its proper height, by tackling already arranged, and four of the iron ribs of the dome will be immediately put in place to sustain it. Probably all of the ribs will be put up during the week, when the Palace will be seen in its proper proportions. Confidence is still entertained that the main part of this immense structure, the body of the building, will be complete by the 1st of June. Over 400 men are employed on it. To-day, the American quarter of the building, which is the north-east corner, adjoining the refreshment saloon, will lie given over to the hands of the Association, that the cases, tables, Ac., for the display of goods may be arranged. The department for machinery, agricultural implements, Ac., which is distinct from this, is not yet prepared. The roof is now nearly complete, except the dome, and the floors are in such afoiward state that fortyeight hours will suffice to finish them, after the dome is up. There is comparatively little more glazing to be done. The galleries are to be faced with an ornamental railing of iron wire, painted white, with gilt rosettes, and lined w ith crimson cloth. The outside of the building will be bronzed, with all the prominent points touched with gold. The effect, when lighted up by the sun, will be very superb. The whole struc-

ture w ill be surrounded w ith a substantial wrought iron fence, (»£ feet in height, to be erected the present week.
