(Inrrespondeneo of the Journal of Commerce. Canton, lolli March, 18f>3. I have nothing to say about business, and write merely to give you the on ilits of the day about the rebellion. It has made great head certainly ; and though it is impossible to say, among the thousand and one rumors, what is correct, I believe we are on the eve of considerable changes. Last night a story was afloat, said to have been brought by an express carrier in eight days, and to have leaked out of the Valium, that Nankin had been taken. I think it extremely probable ; and, if true, the whole affair will be decided ere long. For Kishen, one of the cleverest men in the Empire, is in the vicinity, with a host of Coreans, Mongols, A, Tartars, the best troops in China, and a collision must ensue. On (lie event of the battle depends the fate of the throne ; for I suspect the Kmperor is now in the field with all the men he can raise ; and if defeated now, he must go to the wall, and if victorious, the insurrection is crushed. Of all the stories connected with the affair, none have been so persevered in from the commencement, as that assigning leadership and influence to foreigners ; and there really seem many grounds for the belief. They are called b v many the "Christians" þÿ the "God worshipers," and it is said that they observe Sunday. The latest takes this form: þÿ There are four men, wearing the Chinese dress, but not tnlkingthc Chinese language well, who are at the head ofthe rebel council of war, and without whose

sanction no step is taken. These men are generally supposed to be French Jesuits; and if Catholicism forms an element ofthe combination, the farther North they go the stronger they become, as that religion is more widely diffused in that quarter. Their success in battle against the Imperialists, and the military skill which has characterized some of their movements, give additional strength to the supposition of foreign aid. So long as these disturbances continue, trade must be more or less affected ; but the success of the rebels, I am inclined to think, would revolutionize the whole policy of China, foreign and in-

. ternal ; and we may look for an extension of our privileges and of general commerce. The proposal to legalize the importation of opium, which has been sent by the Emperor to the Chief Council, speaks more loudly than anything else could do, of the poverty of the treasury, and the straits to which he is reduced. The duty fixed is high, and though as much smuggling would be carried on then as now, the revenue would be augmented by the numerous " squeezes" that would be made in Chinese style.

Wilmer ami Smith's European Times, May 1(1, 1 8.73. The Emigration Trade. þÿ During the last month more emigrants have left the port of Liverpool than in the corresponding month of any former year. The returns of the government showthat, in the month ending Saturday last, between 27,000 and 28,000 emigrants left the Mersey for the land ofthe stranger. By far the greater proportion of these have been shipped for America. The passenger trade to the Australian ports has experienced a check, owing to the unfavourable accounts recently received. Notwithstanding this, however, 20 vessels, of an aggregate tonnage of 17,470 tons have cleared out for Melbourne, Adelaide, Geelong, and Sydney within the last few weeks. Many of the finest packet-ships in the world are now loading at our docks, and some of them w ill take their departure in a few days. The Banker's Daughter, with 400 emigrants from the government depot at Birkenhead, will sail shortly; she will be followed in the course of the month by three large ships with passengers from the same place. Among the private ships loading for Australia are þÿ and Co.'s " Eagle" line of packets: the the Falcon, one of Messrs. Gibbs, Bright, Lochiel, of Messrs. I'ilkington and Wilson's " White Star" line ; the Indian Queen, sister ship to the Marco l'olo ; and one of Messrs. Baines and Co.'s " Black Ball" line; the Star of the East, one of Messrs. Millers and Thompson's "Golden" line; the Ann Itolzberg, of the " Fox" line ; the Alabama, and others.

Present to an African Potentate. þÿ A magnificent piece of silver plate, weighing upwards of 13.40 ounces, intended as a present for one of the African potentates on the Gold Coast, has been manufactured by Messrs. Charles Taylor and Son, of Bristol, by order of Mr. John Wood, African merchant, and was despatched during the past week for the coast of Africa in the ship Hope. The present consists of a silver hip and shower bath, most elaborately chased and ornamented, and standing between seven and eight feet in height. The bath stands on a roll foot, ornamented with lotus leaves, the back chased with armorial bearings, with the lion and nnicorn as supporters. The elbow rests upon two elegantly chased scrolls. From the bath rise four massive and ornamented silver pillars, fitting into rich foliage sockets, and supporting a Hanged tulipshaped silver cistern, capable of holding ten or twelve gallons of water, ornamented with an edging of lotus leaves and fluting, the whole richly chased in relief. The pump is very handsomely finished off with a twisted serpent handle. The curtains are of rich crimson satin damask, lined with oiled silk. The whole is enclosed in a mahogany case, clipped with silver mountings, and forming altogether a most unique article of workmanship in silver. The cost of the article, we are informed, is little short of T 1000. þÿ Ibid.

(Concluded.) The Minister of Finance : þÿ Both in regard to the general remarks, and to several of his special remarks, I can in a great measure declare myself agreed with the honourable member, who has just spoken. I agree, that it is desirable, that the Colonies should, as far as possible, govern themselves ; but I cannot express a hope, that it could take place at once, or in a very short time, for it ought not to be done in such a way as to create new expenses. The natural way is, as partially done for some years, to do away with the offices, as far as possible, when they become vacant, and to let the functions go over to communal authorities. The most proper beginning to place the Colonies on their own footing, and to enable them to have a weighty influence on their own affairs, has no doubt been made by the Colonial Law, and 1 think, that what has come from the Colonial Council, the important and significant reports which we have received from them after so short a time, is a good sign that the said Council will be of great use to the islands. It has been my constant desire, and I have partly succeeded in this budget, to restrict the number of public offices as much as possible. On looking at the Budget, as it is now, not to speak of what it used to be before, it is clear that those small islands have a too large administration, and that greater simplicity may yet be expected ; it is however more easy to complicate than again to simplify business, as will be understood by those

acquainted with such affairs, and I have more particularly found this to be the case by the reforms I desired to effect at St. Thomas. With regard to that island, it was remarked by the honourable member, who just sat down, that it might be possible to insert a clause in this budget, with the view of limiting the term of the Commandant's office to a part of the year ; I must say, that my thoughts have been the same. 1 have sent an order to the Colonics about the same time as this budget came out ; on the impression of the considerations connected with this budget. I have ordered measures to be taken to do away with the office of Commandant on the 1st October, or at latest on the 1st of January next. As far as regards the personal question, I have free hands, no person havinga permanent appointment to the said office. I am not so free in regard to the management of the official business, as to say for certain, that the change will take place on the 1st of October ; I hope it, but, at all events, the order has been given, and will be executed so that it shall take place on the 1st of January. 1 have not ventured to insert anything about this proposed economy in the present budget, because I was not certain that the change of business might cause some expense for a short time, and T could wish to have i or 1 of the Commandant's revenues at my disposal f r that purpose. I had hoped in the present budget to have adopted a plan for the new organisation of the administration at St. Thorr.as, in conformity with the wishes

of the Colonial Council, I have however not succeeded, and on that account it has become necessary to begin anew, by a ministerial order, as just stated. I have besides adopted some other measures, and I have caused one of the public functionaries to be requested to petition to retire from office, by which a saving of some amount would be effected ; however as the case has not yet occurred, it will not be proper to deviate from the sums specified in the budget. It has also been intended to reduce the expenses of the Court of Appeal, which cannot be entirely done away with, but is more costly than I consider necessary to secure a safe administration of justice ; however, I cannot devise a final plan, until I have conferred with the Minister of Justice. From what I have indicated, omitting several points, it is not improbable that the next year's budget may show soine more retrenchments ; a more thorough-going economy will not take place, before the large military force can be reduced, (hear), that is the point on which it depends, and which the Govt, at the same time must treat with great carc, and cannot take the responsibility to decide without hearing the opinion of the Colonial Council, whether it is advisable or not. From its relation and position in the colonies, that Council has the greatest interest to make the expenditures as moderate as possible, and I do not doubt, that as it has already now supported the initiative of the Governor to limit the station of the man-of-

war, so they will take the initiative, or support the initiative of the Governor, to reduce the expenses of the troops. This matter has however uot advanced far enough to allow of a further proposal, than already made in this budget, and

3 <\ e Ui :D H ATI 8« which is founded on a calculation of the time, which it takes to supply the vacancies, the force being larger on paper, than in reality, some of the men being on the voyage between Europe and the Islands. As far as regards the Brig-of-war, I am glad to hear that the honorable member is agreeing with me, that the expenses of the station ought not to be borne by the colonies. As a part of the Colonial budget of former times, that fixed station was of moment, when pirates infested those seas, but now it is different, and with the troops in the colonies, there is not the least fear, that they would be molested by pirates. The danger now lies in the social condition of the colonics themselves, against which the Brig can do little, but the troops more. It is however thought proper to have the full force also of the man-ofwar, at the time when the measures, resulting from the deliberation of the Colonial Council, are to be put in force. That is the reason, why I have charged half a year's expense for the station of the man-of-war on this budget, at the desire of the Governor ; but next year 1 hope to come to the result not to charge any part of it on that budget, believing that it will not be required for the sake of the colonies ; and if the flag is still shewn there, it is not specially for the sake of the colonies, but because it is proper that the Danish flag should occasionally be seen in foreign ports and also in the colonics, and not only on a brig or small vessel of war, but sometimes on a larger

one. However, that belongs to the resort of the Minister of Marine, and whatever is required for the honor and benefit of the country will be charged on the budget of the navy and not to the colonies. By granting the sum required in this form, it will no doubt be more satisfactory to the navy also, than if left to the charge of the colonies. It has been desired that the steam communication between St. Croix and St. Thomas might be established at an earlier period, than proposed in the budget. From elucidations received by the ministry here, it appears unlikely that it could take place, even if more money were granted, and 1 should therefore not advise giving more than the sum already charged. This steam communication is more particularly to be recommended as it will enable the Government in the West Indies to centralize the administration, and do away with the local Government at St. Thomas, and by granting the sum required, it will be the means of further saving. With regard to the additional sum asked for the Governor, I beg to remind the house, that in a former budget a similar sum was granted the predecessor of the present Governor. When he was appointed, it was proposed to try if a smaller sum would possibly do, and T could have no objection to make the experiment. Tt happens so, that the present incumbent is peculiarly adapted for it, because he is personally and unusually disinterested and economical, and you may fully depend upon his judgment on the sufficiency or

insufficiency of the salary, and the more, because he is quite decided by motives of a more private nature, not to remain in the colonies more than one year over the time at first stipulated by him. I am very sorry that it is the case, because there is reason to be highly satisfied with his conduct, and I think it is appreciated in the colonics. His opinion can be depended on, because he will derive very little personal advantage from the increased salary. It can be easily understood, why he would not propose an increased salary in a budget prepared by himself, anil from the same motives he has abstained from touching this matter in his official correspondence, but 1 am nevertheless, fully aware that he considers the present pay of the Governor insufficient. It might perhaps not make a difference with regard to his remaining, if the $2,000 in question were granted or not, this present year ; but it is highly important for me, that it should pass, because when that appointment was to be made on the last vacancy, I experienced great difficulty in finding a proper person for it, which difficulty will be increased, when it is known that a governor, both moderate in his demands and of saving habits, declares the salary to be insufficient. The reforms and retrenchments in the colonies, which have become necessary since 1848, are mainly depending on the person of the Governor, and to save in this instance, would not be right. I am happy to learn that the lion, member who spoke

last, is inclined to support my views in this instance. The Minister of Marine : þÿ With regard to what has been said about the station of a man-ofwar in the West Indies, I can mainly refer to the words of the Minister of Finance. It is of very little moment to me where the money-grant conies from and on what budget the sum is charged ; but I cannot abstain from remarking, that it appears questionable whether it would be right to

take measures here, which would make it doubtful if a man-of-war were to be sent out or not to that station. I do believe, that as long as we have colonies, they ought not to be left without naval defence (hear!) and intercourse. It has been said that the steam communication now to be established, was meant to replace the defence by the man-of-war, but I decidedly disagree from that, although considering the steamer to deserve all possible encouragement and support. Its usefulness will mainly depend upon its ability to undertake all the carriage and a regular packet service between the islands, but it cannot be a man-of-war at the same time. The navy will be quite satisfied, to have in view, that it is not always a small vessel, but sometimes a larger ship of war, that is to be sent out on such a cruise ; and it will be highly useful to show the flag also in other ports, besides those in the AA'est Indies. I would consider it right that the man-of-war sent out on this yearly expedition, and which we must insist upon not giving up, should always, either first or last, go to the \V. I. seas. I believe it will always prove useful to have a manof-war there. Mu. Flage: þÿ It cannot be necessary for me to assure the honorable Minister of Marine, that T have not meant that a steam packet, with one or two guns, could in all cases compensate for a brig-of-war of the size generally sent out ; but have believed, that when the man-of-war was dispensed with, it might be of use to have a steamer,

manned with a few additional hands and having a few cannon on board. I do not agree with the lion. Minister, that we should have a brig iu the AVest Indies for the defence of the islands, and T do uot know in what case they could be defended by such a brig. I observed, that the honorable member from the 4th district of Maribo (Bishop Monrad) said "hear" but I do not know how far he is acquainted with naval history, and if he will undertake to defend the islands with such a vessel, L do not think that the Minister of Marine can do it. The lion. Minister of Finance said, that there was no fear of pirates, and I therefore cannot see the necessity of having a brig-of-war on the station. A word, dropped from the mouth of the lion. Minister of Finance, was eagerly me a little, as he thought that " for the honor of caught by the hon. Marine Minister, and alarmed the country" a larger ship ought to be sent out that " honor," is as well on board a brig-of-war I believe the hon. Minister will agree with me, as a frigate, and as trade and other circumstances arc now in the world, I believe that we can be fully satisfied to hoist the flag on a brig, and I would not wish to be the cause of now at once sending out a frigate, instead of a twelve or sixteen gun vessel. The hon. Finance Minister has advised to send out a vessel in October, but 1 should wish to leave it to the Governor and the Commander of the brig-of-war to decide, if it would not be advisable to let the brig visit other ports, and not remain constantly in the AA'est In-

dies, or bind it by strict orders to St. Croix, even iu the event of a fever epidemic. The Minister of Marine: þÿ I believe that the last proposal of the hon. member has always been followed ; the brig ot war is not constantly near our islands, but visits different foreign ports. There was much sickness last year, but we have had a number of previous years without the least sickness, and not lost a single man. I ain quite agreed with the hon. member about the propriety of shewing the flag in foreign ports. As far as regards the defence, it is very true, that one vessel could not defend the islands in case of an attack by a foreign foe, but the mere presence of a man-of-war is of importance, even in times of entire peace ; and we should not, from too much economy, do away with an opportunity to show the flag with dignity at a place, where we have a station. It is not necessary to have a vessel constantly on the station ; I have for many years not been in the AA'est Indies, but T think I am right in insisting on, that the islands are not entirely deprived of the presence of a man-of-war in future. At the proposal of an hon. member, it was resolved to appoint a Committee of Five to report on the Colonial Budget.

The annexed communication is from a gentleman who has had much experience are 2£ of inches in the manufacture ofiron work, and also in the direction and management of Railroads. For the Journal ofCommerce. Causes ol' ICuilroud Accident. Messrs Hali.ock, Butler andIIai.e: þÿ Gentlemen : þÿ The recent calamity at Norwalk has aroused the attention of the public to the causes of rail way accidents, to an unusual degree. I wish to say a few words respecting two classes of these causes ; þÿ imperfections in the road bed, and in the machinery, particularly in the cars. The road bed, if the soil is clay or loam, should be covered with gravel two

feet thick. The ties should he 36 to 42 inches longer than the width of the track, not less that seven inches square, and of sound hard timber. The iron should weigh at least 691b. to the yard, should he tough and fibrous, and be secured to the ties by chairs weighing 20 lb. or more. To show how far these particulars actually exist, I will state what occurred recently under myown observation on a very important road. On or about the 8th of March last, I was traveling from Albany to Buffalo, and was about 30 miles West of Utica, when the rear cars of the train were suddenly thrown from the track as we were going 40 miles an hour. We were on a straight line, and the engine being instantly reversed, the cars were not | turned over, and no personal injury was sustained. While the employees of the Company were getting the cars on the track, I walked back a few rods to examine the cause of the accident. I had been told by the conductor that a rail had broken, and that the engineer, feeling it break as the engine passed over it, had stopped the train. I found jive rails broken within five rods of each other, and all of them, except the first, evidently by the cars jerking over them. Three of them were broken in such a manner that I could take up one of the pieces and examine the fracture. In each case I found the iron of a crystalinc structure like cast iron, and entirely without fibre. I examined the other track, and found the ties very light, and apparently old

chairs was broken, and found that the rail would spring up and down with the motion of my foot. As a gang of men were repairing the broken track, I pointed out this chair to one of them, who told me that it was much better than many on the road, and that the quality of the road bed was so bad, from want of gravel, that it was very difficult to keep it in order. In two or three hours the cars were replaced, the road patched up, and we passed on. I mention these facts because I think it due to public safety, and because I think that a company whose stock is worth 176, can afford to keep their road in good order. I also think it is for their interest; for, if a serious accident occurred, and the above facts were proved before a jury, the damages would not be very small. Every bar of iron, of the quality of those which 1 examined, ought to he immediately taken up and replaced. 2. Imperfection of machinery. Almost

the breaking of wheels and axles. The wheels, if made of cast iron, should be quality equal to Salisbury, well chilled and tough. The axles for a passenger-train should be made of fagoted or scrap iron, and should weigh at least lbs. and be not less than 34 inches in diameter in the journal. But, with the exception of the new cars on the New York and New Haven Road, I do not believe that there are thirty cars in New England and New York which have axles this size. Almost all of them diameter in the journal. The strength is as the square of the diameter, and of course of axle 2$ inches diameter, has just half the strength of one of 3J inches, and is at least ten times more likely to break. Most of them are ot puddled iron, which is most inferior in quality to the scrap or fagoted axles. The result of using such axles is found in the late "accident" on the Tauntonroatl, and in that by which President Fierce was rendered childless. The difference in the expense of the best and poorest axles is less than one hundred dollars to a car. Perhaps at some future time, a jury which decides how much a Railroad Company shall

pay for limbs, broken in sympathy with an axle, will cause the axle to lie brought into court, and will decide whether it was sufficient for safety. It ought to be remembered and felt by tbe directors of railroads, and by the community, that roads and machinery which were tolerably safe when twenty miles an hour was satisfactory speed, and fifteen ton engines answered very well, are not adapted to a speed of forty miles an hour, and to engines like the " Addison Gilmore." It will he remembered by many readers of this paper, that, early in the year 1829, in commemoration of the Nuptials ol' our present Sovereign, then Prince of Denmark, a Fund was raised by subscription, having for its object the training of teachers for these Islands. The amount subscribed by some gentlemen, together with the contributions, during the space of ten years, freely given by the Burgher Council in behalf of its constituents, amounted in 1838 to $7,218 52 ; which amount, if suffered to accumulate on simple interest, would amount to about $13,700 and on compound interest to about $17,300 in the present year. In 1838 it was decided on placing this amount on interest, until, it should finally be settled in what manner it should be applied. It was accordingly lent out some years after to the Proprietor of an Estate, where, we believe it still rests. It appears somewhat strange, that, there ever should have been a question as to the manner of applying this money, and that this question should have been allowed to remain unsettled to the present time, When, the object lor which the Fund was raised, was so definitely stated ; and even a name in accordance therewith given, viz : þÿ Fund Tor (-iliieuling Tracliers lor Ui« Danish West India Elþÿands. The question must naturally arise, could no youths be found fit to bo educated for this purpose ? To judge from the present time, we sec no lack of youths with good native abilities, from whose minds it would only be necessary to re-

move the rubbish in order to produce some pretty strong intellects. This, therefore, could not have been the reason why the benevolent intentions of the subscribers to this Fund have never been carried out. We are aware that the interest of this capital has, for some years, been applied to defray the expenses of the Danish School. This, nevertheless, can no more be considered as the fulfillment of the intention of the Donors, than if the money had been applied to any other purpose. In our opinion, such a use of the interest should only be made, when it would be impossible to apply it to its legitimate use ; which has never even been tried, consequently, cannot be declared to be impossible. We intend these observations merely to call the attention of the Burgher Council to the case ; for we arc so strong in the conviction of the good intentions of our present (lovernment, as to feel confident, that, il this case be brought before their notice, in a proper manner, it will receive all the attention it merits. In conclusion, we express it as our humble opinion, that it would be no difficult task, to hold out as an inducement to the children of poor parents attending the public schools, that, at certain periods the one who is most deserving will be chosen from among the rest and be educated as a Teacher. An oi.d Subscriber. Juno 15, 1853.

The table which wo saw most powerfully acted upon was of mahogany, solid, not veneered nor inlaid, about three or four feet long, and two feet wide ; without castors, and standing on a carpet, in a room with a fire About six persons, standing, placed the palms of their bands flat upon the table, rather near the edge ; every þÿperson two s thumbs touched eaeli other, and the little finger of each þÿone s band touched the little finger of bis or her neighbor, forming a complete chain. At the end of that time, the table visibly and tangibly began slowly to move : before this, however, it was agreed, but this we feel more hesitation in recording as a positive condition of the experiment, that some of the party should join in forming a fixed determination as to the direction in which the table should move. However this may be, the table moved from one

room to another, and, after a short pause, back again, at a moderate pace ; it also turned round several times at a more rapid pace, and, apparently, at the will of 2 or 3 of the party who appeared more powerful than the rest. power the table moved with only a single pair of hands laid upon one end of it. The proposition was received with rapturous applause, and a happy thought of the þÿleader s at once selected the national chaunt, whose burthen (sure to meet with most general sympathy) is, Britons never sliull bo slaves, Up the winding staircase, six or seven stories high, and through the long, deserted rooms of that factory, such a chorus had never resounded before; and its effect Wits al most electrical, for the employer, turning on his heel with an

Wre have left but little space to notice the debates in both houses on Tuesday, the 26th ultimo, on the principle of the contract packet service. It will he seen that a new system is to be entered upon. Contracts are to be taken for short periods, and competition encouraged. On Friday morning last, at Estate Judiths Fancy, after a few þÿdays illness, Captain F. \V. Bent/.on, Colonial Aid to Ills Excellency the Governor, and 1st þÿKing C s lerk in the Government Secreþÿtary Office s ; aged 45 years. As a tribute to the memory of Captain Bent/.on, we are called upon to express a few words, not without the deepest regret for the loss of a respectable and beloved citizen, whose superior qualities shone so resplendent, whose kindness and unassuming manners had endeared him to all classes in this community, and whose death is universally regretted. His high intellectual talents had earned for him a respectable situation, in which lie, for a great number of years, discharged all his duties with zeal and punctuality, giving entire satisfaction to all ; and his charity, which knew no bounds, had oft relieved the wants of the widow, orphan and destitute. llis remains were taken from Judiths Fancy, on Saturday morning, followed by a large concourse of the most respectable inhabitants of this place, both military and civil, planters from all parts of the country, and a great number of peasants, and conveyed to the Burial Ground of this town, where they were buried amid the tears of surrounding relatives, friends and domestics. The news of his death will be a sore afflict ion to his disconsolate widow and children, who are at present in Europe, and to his numerous friends abroad.

IVilmer and þÿSmith European s Times , June 16, 1853. The Danish Ministry has carried the day in most of the elections for the Second Chamber of the Diet. It is now, therefore, probable that the succession hill, in conformity with the protocol of London, will be accepted by the new parliament. The most eminent men of the late chamber declined the contest which has just terminated, perceiving that the Government was determined to carry its point, and not wishing to put the constitution to a strain too severe. 'I'lie customs line of the Danish monarchy was removed to the Elbe on the 1st instant, and fixed there. The anniversary of the constitution was celebrated as a day of general rejoicing at Copenhagen on the 7th. Business was suspended. Processions advanced upon the palace with deputations to congratulate the King, and at night the city was illuminated.

The arrival of the West India Mail steam-ship Orinoco two days beyond the period assigned to the voyage has afforded occasion for another attack on the administration þÿof the Royal Mail Company. 'Fhe omission laid to their charge is in what has been termed the detention of the Orinoco at 8t. Thomas two days beyond the proper date of departure, by the irregularity of the intercolonial service has been performed by the now packet the Esk. This vessel, it is stated, is unfit for the service on which she is employed ; but that we are credibly informed is no fault of the directors of the

3 U\ <8 Ji 'G> li A 'T 1 3, company. The Esk is placed on that portion of the line from Honduras to Jamaica, and on the arrival of the mail at that island, it is re-conveyed with the Jamaica mail to 8t. Thomas, at which place it meets the steamer to England. By the estimated speed, the Esk should perform eight with and four miles against tide. She is an auxiliary screw-ship, built in 184!), and though the average performance required of her is so low, it is well known that she has repeatedly done 250 miles in 24 hours, and performed 10 knots per hour under canvas alone. 'Flic Esk had undergone a thorough refit, and this was her first trip on the Honduras route. She had been previously employed on the Nassau and Bio de Janeiro and River Plate stations, on both of which she had given satisfaction to the public; and her non-appearance at the appointed time at Jamaica on Ibis occasion is solely attributable to her commander, who attempted to steam against the strong stream of the Gulf and a bead wind, instead of shaping bis course towards the Island of Cuba, and thus taking advantage of the set of the current and the winds which would have favoured his ship when on that coast. It was the first voyage of the Captain in question, a first-rate seaman, who bad commanded one of the þÿDunbar s large ships, but who forgot in this instance that he commanded an auxiliary screw vessel. This is a common fault with the commanders of screw-vessels ; they think that because they are in charge of steamers they must make the sails aux-

iliary to the screw þÿ thus reversing the order of things. We believe the company have determined to supersede him, though this is to be regretted, for by all accounts he is a worthy officer. The yellow fever, during the last six months, lias made such havoc among the officers of the company, that it has been a difficult matter to meet the supply to fill up vacancies with masters or mates possessing an intimate knowledge of the navigation among the isles of the West Indies, and thence to the American continent. Then, again, the section of the service on which the Esk is temporarily employed should have been supplied w ith a new ship, which, according to the terms of contract with the builder, ought to have been on the station ere this, but she is now in a forward state. When it is considered that the intercolonial service of the West India Company is a sort of Chinese puzzle þÿ vessels starting from some 28 ports, and all meeting punctually at a given terminus, and that the Esk was the only packet not to her time on this last start, there is room for excuse ; but when that vessel is superseded by a more powerful steamer we may expect this portion of the route to be more expeditiously undertaken. þÿ'I lie same company are taxed with allowing the news from the Pacific by the American steamers to reach Liverpool tenu de Monbijou, for the purpose of , in less time than the mail from the West Indies to Southampton. The Liverpool remonstrants should understand that the

packets from the United States laud their mails in the Mersey, and they are on the spot to receive the news. According to this theory the merchants ot Southampton ought to complain that the American mail is received in Liverpool, and letters delivered there before the distribution at their port. But are the kingdom? Liverpool merchants the only in ones Have we none London? in the The delivery in the capital should be the proper gunge of success. And we have authority for stating that since the
transatlantic ships of the Royal Mail Company, the South Pacific mails have, in every instance but two, and those two can be explained by the mail arriving

after the departure of their steamers from Mexico, been brought to tins country before those forwarded via New York. When the company first undertook the mail service in 1840 but very little experience had been obtained of ocean steam navigation; but the vessels they then built were universally admitted at that time to be the finest constructed ; and it speaks highly in their favour, that during a service extending over 13 years there has been only one instance noted of their vessels not starting from England at the appointed time. In 184!) their contract was renewed, and the Brazil mail contracted for. On the renewal of their contract they immediately ordered a new fleet of most magnificent ships ; and in less than four years they have had built for them the Magdalena of 2,404 registered tons ; the Orinoco, of 2901 tons; the Parana, of 2,943 tons; the Amazon, of 2,900 tons; the Demerara, of 2,900 tons ; and the \trato, of 2,720 tons; all of which vessels are nearly equal in tonnage, some registering higher than the Great Britain. Besides those vessels they have purchased the La Plata, of 2,404 tons ; and on the 8th of June the Solent, 1,781 tons, will be launched from the yard of Mr. White, at Cowes, the celebrated shipbuilder. Until it was decided that tin; contract should be renewed, the company could not, with safety to their shareholders, venture upon an extension of their fleet ; for though amateurs do not mind risking a few millions in a speculation, the directors of the West

India Company had gathered sufficient experience to convince them that a steam company, working full-powered paddlewheel steamers, could not go on w ithout state aid. 'Fhe problem of auxiliarypropelled steamers has yet to be tried, but it is the opinion of well informed men that unless the screw is used merely as an auxiliary all screw companies must in the end fail. Whenever a long voyage has been performed by a screwvessel under steam the whole voyage the loss has been very great, and the voyage to Australia of the Great Britain has sunk no less than jCIO.OOO. Every person must wish tor the success of cheapl v-propclled vessels, but the proprietors of screw-vessels must look at the matter in a mercantile light. From the St. Thomas Times , July 2, 1853. FIB E IN TOWN! Bi twki n two and three o'clock yesterday morning an alarm of Fire aroused the Inhabitants of our Town, and on proceeding to the spot it was found that the devouring element had lull possession of a range of small stores on the Lot No. Ill »V 17, the property of Mr. A. It. Ligoett. Mr. IIoykks, old and Silver Smith ; Mr. Iaiincke, (1 Clock and Watch Maker; and Mr. Livikn, Tobacconist, were the principal occupants of the range. One of the stores had also just been occupied by the Manager of a Uosinorama, where it is supposed the Fire originated. This, however, is still a matter of doubt. Neither of the parties above-mentioned was enabled to save anything, in fact each has sustained a total loss. Great fears were also entertained at one period of the tire that the adjoining dwelling and store of Mr. Delvalle would have been destroyed, but providentially there was scarcely any wind þÿ the flame burning as erect as that of a candle. The noble and timely exertions of Mr. Thomas II. Wood þÿ who at great risk ascended a parapet wall, and courageously directed a copious stream of water against the East shutters of the aforesaid dwelling stayed the progress of the fire, which þÿ eventually subsided. The Pipe held by Mr. Wood belongs to the Engine of the Military, who by keeping her supplied with water caused her to produce the good result. An equal amount of danger attended the dwelling of Mrs. Vetter, at the other end þÿ the windows of which are burnt to charcoal on the back

þÿ and the building was saved only by the daring and praise-worthy conduct of a few gentlemen, who kept the shutters constantly wet by dashing water against them. Among the most prominent of them we can mention Mr. Christ! an Muller. We are happy in having it in our power to state that every exertion was manifested by the entire crowd to aid in extinguishing the Fire, which once threatened to grow into an extensive Conflagration ! We feel exceedingly indebted to the Commander of the French War-Steamer Le Grandeur lor having promptly sent on shore an Officer and 21 men, with an Engine, who rendered invaluable service on the North part of the building as it continued to burn. This Engine attracted the attention of a number of persons, owing to its compactness, with the power of throwing so large a volume of water. The Town Engines repaired to the spot, but, as on other occasions, were indifferently served, and more by volunteers than by the established Corps. Having given an account of the Fire as far as we know, now turn our attention to a circumstance, which elicits not only our sympathy, in the shape of words, but also in a more substantial manner. We allude to the ruined condition of

the sufferers, who are artizans, and being deprived of their tools and capital for prosecuting their avocations, are temporarily debarred from earning a livelihood. One of the sufferers has now for the third time been divested of his all, by means of this ruthless element. We hope the St. Thomas community, so ready to aid at all times out-of-doors sufferers, will not be less benevolent when their fellow-townsmen are stricken down by misfortune. We understand that a List lies open at the þÿSavings Bank for signatures. The loss is computed to exceed $10,000. The 11. M. S. Orinoco also sent ou shore an Officer and a number of men, with buckets, books, small ladders, ij-e. The Superintendent of the Company likewise had his men on the spot.

The Manehcster Guardian, dune 4, 1853. þÿ TABLE þÿMOVING CONVERSA- ZIONE AT THE ATHEN EIJM. On Thursday evening, a conversazione, having for its object the arrivþÿ ing at some safe conclusion concerning table þÿmoving and its causes, was held in the library hall of the Athenaeum, which had been engaged by a committee of gentlemen, for that purpose. The audience, which was numerous, was accommodated with seats round the room, the central portion being occupied by seven tables of various forms and sizes, all of which were during the evening experimented upon. The Rev. II. II Jones, F. R. A. 8. was called to the chair, and in opening the proceedings, said that it appeared to him that the phenomenon of table turning must necessarily be the result either of collusion, illusion, or of the action of some mysterious and hitherto almost unknown and unrecognised force. That it was not the result of collusion was, lie thought, proved by the number of intelligent and respectable persons who were ready to vouch for the reality of the facts. That it might lie the result of illusion or selldelusion on the part of the experimenters, wtis just possible, but, perhaps, not very probable. It was just possible that there might be such tin adhesion between the lingers of the experimenters and the table, such a power of friction as, gradually accumulating, should he suliicicnt to overcome the inertia of the matter contained in the table, find cause it to move. Some might think that there could not he this amount of friction or

adhesiveness, without the experimenters being conscious of it. He was not so sure of that. When persons bad held their lingers in a certain position for ;i considerable length of time. Ilnur lingers became comparatively benumbed, anti it was just possible that they might unconsciously exercise such an amount of force as might move the table. Then came the third and last question : supposing the phenomenon not to In the result of either of these causes, could it be that it was produced by the action ol some mysterious and unknown force, hitherto unrecognised 1 If so, we must suppose that this force issued from the hands and lingers of the experimenters, and that it (lowed to the right or left in obedience to their will. þÿ Mr. W. G. Gintv moved the appointment of a committee, to have the direction of the experiments, and report upon them. The motion was seconded and unanimously agreed to. The chairman then invited ladies and gentlemen who were willing to experiment npon tables, to take their places, tind in it few minutes till the tat.les lint one were surrounded by experimenters, including persons of various ages, and both sexes. The experiments commented nt eight þÿo clock. The first table which moved was a round one, nbotit three feet in diameter, standing upon three legs, without castors, and having a leather top. At this table, four ladies took their places, and in five minutes it

began to turn rapidly, the ladies running round with it. After several stoppages, for which the experimenters could not account, the table moved round so rapidly that several of the ladies appeared to be getting giddy, and two of them became so much alarmed that they discontinued the experiment. These ladies had simply placed their hands upon the table, without touching those of each other. After this experiment, the chairman suggested that it should be repeated, the ladies having tissue paper placed between their hands and the table, to prevent the effects of friction. This was tried for fourteen minutes, with three ladies only (the other two being too much alarmed to take part), and failed. The other two ladies were then induced to join the circle, and in three minutes the table moved. Upon examination, it was found that the tissue paper had been wetted by perspiration, and had adhered to the table. It had, therefore, failed to counteract the possible effects of friction, and proved nothing. The second table which moved was a large and heavy round one, of polished wood, about four feet six inches in diameter, and weighing about 1 0,1 lbs., having a pillar and three claws, to each of which there was a castor. Hound it sat eight gentlemen, who formed the circle in the usual manner, touching each þÿother slittle lingers, lint not bringing the thumbs of their own hands into contact. At twenty-five minutes past eight þÿo clock (when the experiment had been conducted for 25 min-

utes). tliis table began to move slowly from right to left ; and with some stoppages, it performed about two revolutions in that direction. It t hen stopped, and after waiting some minutes, the experimenters, w ho had previously willed that it should move from right to left, willed that it should move in a contrary direction. In a minute or two, motion recommenced, and the table moved so rapidly in the direction intended, that the gentlemen who had previously risen from their seats, were obliged to run round with it ; and its revolutions did not cease until one person, feeling giddy, withdrew his hands and broke the circle. It was observed that this table turned upon one of the three claws as an axis ; this claw however did not remain perfectly stationary, and the circumference of the table described a series of eccentric circles. þÿ After the performance of these experiments, l)r. Ilraid said there had been some most unexceptionable experiments. They had seen two tables turn, and his conviction was that the motion arose from what Dr. Carpenter called the ideo-motor pow er. The mind being concentrated tor a length of time upon an idea, it at last began to act upon the muscular system. This was not a voluntary act, and might even be in opposition to volition. lie was satisfied, so far as he had seen, that this was the true solution of the matter ; that the ladies and gentlemen were not conscious that they exercised any effort, and that the effect arose from this unconscious

muscular action. In order to test whether or not the motion was caused by electricity, he suggested that a wire should be laid upon the tables, and that instead of touching the table the experimenters should hold this wire. It the motion arose from electricity, it would take place under these circumstances; if it was the result of muscular action the effect ol that action would be on the wire, and not on the table. þÿ The experiment was accordingly ' tried. A piece of this wire was laid round the þÿladies table; it was twisted into a loop bet ween each of the operators, and was then held by the ladies who had previously operated so successfully. The hands of the

& <B & <1> 1 A VT 3 3, ladies did not touch the table. They maintained their positions for half an hour without success, and then abandoned the attempt. They then placed their fingers upon the table, and in about a minute it turned rapidly. þÿ The third table which moved was a similar one to that which was moved by the ladies. Five persons sat at it, and at thirty-seven minutes after eight it turned rapidly from right to left. These persons had formed the circle in the ordinary manner, with only the little fingers touching. When the table began to move, some ol' the bystanders thought that some of the experimenters were exercising pressure, and, therefore, suggested that they should cross their hands, as it was thought that in this position they would he unable to exercise any force upon the table. This was done, and the table afterwards moved rapidly from right to left, and left to right. The last table to turn was a square one of mahogany, about six teet long by four wide, standing upon four legs. At eight þÿo clock, eight gentlemen and two ladies sat down to this table and continued the experiment without success until thirty-five minutes past nine, when they discontinued it. Seven gentlemen and five ladies, including three of those who had previously been so successful, then sat dow n, and in about a quarter of an hour they moved the table a short distance. The circle was then broken by one of the party, and the table stopped. At nine þÿo clock, the gentlemen who had previously moved the large round table,

formed the circle as before, but without allowing their fingers to touch the table. They tried this experiment for ten minutes, hut without success. The ('hairman suggested that, in order to prevent the effects of friction, a table should he smeared with olive oil, upon which the i experimenters should place their lingers. In accordance with this suggestion, a belt of oil about live inches wide from the edge was made upon one of the round tables. Six gentlemen then sat down and in about twenty minutes the table moved. The large round table which had been the second to move was then smelired with oil upon the wooden rim, and the same eight gentlemen who had previously experimented again sat down to it. In this instance they formed the circle as before, but only the tips ol' their lingers touched the table. They began their experiment at a quarter past nine, and at one minute before ten þÿo clock the table made part of a revolution from right to left. It afterwards moved in different directions, according to the will of the gentlemen experimenting upon it, up to a quarter past ten þÿo clock, when they desisted. In the course of this experiment these gentlemen were much disturbed by the pressure of the audience upon them; and by other proceedings. Whenever their attention was thus distracted, the table stopped. The Chairman said that no importance could he attached to the result of this experiment, as he saw the thumb of one of the operators upon the edge of the table. All the gentlemen

engaged in the experiment denied that they had placed their thumbs in this position; and a bystander assured us that though the thumb of one gentleman was very near the edge of the table, yet it did not actually touch it. This gentleman was in a better position for observing than the chairman, who was on the platform, and he was laying great attention to the experiment. Several requests were made to the chairman to point out the gentleman whose thumb was upon the edge of the table ; but the chairman only replied that he had no doubt the gentlemen believed that they were acting fairly, and that he

had not thought of charging them with doing otherwise. We have hitherto spoken only of successful experiments but there were three tables which were in vain attempted to be turned. One of these was a mahogany Pembroke table, and the party who experimented upon it consisted of five gentlemen. Another table (resembling that with which the ladies were so successful) which was at first unoccupied, was afterwards taken possession of by a party of seven gentlemen. In forming the circle, they not only touched the little fingers of' each other, but brought their own thumbs into contact. The result of this was that their hands were placed in a circle very near the centre of the table top, and not as in the other cases round its circumference. These gentlemen continued their experiment for some time, but the table did not move. The third unsuccessful experiment was with a small round table, at which five gentlemen remained seated for an hour and thirty-five minutes without producing any client. In the top of this table there was a crack, and some of the experimenters seemed to think tiiat this had prevented the success of the attempt. The chairman, upon being appealed to, said that he did not imagine that it would have any effect. þÿ The chairman, before leaving the chair, said that lie had come into that room without any prejudice; but that, from what he had seen and heard, he believed that the phenomena resulted entirely IrOm muscular action, by the power of friction, lie could not for a moment believe in

the emanation of an occult and hitherto unknow n force exercising such a decided effect upon a mass of brute matter as had that night been manifested. þÿ Dr. liraid, in moving a vote of thanks to the chairman, said, that if we considered the reciprocal action of the mind upon matter, we had a key to the whole mystery. It was a eerlain law that the mind, being concentrated for any lenrDi ot time upon any part of the hotly, changed the physical action of that part. If there was an idea that the table sh ihl move in a given direction, that idea would, without a conscious effort of volition þÿ without the person believing tliiit lie was exercising any effort at all, produce the effect. þÿ The vote of thanks was unanimously adopted, and the proceedings terminated about half-past ten, having lasted three hours. þÿ We have not space in which to notice anv of the statements we heard as to the sensations of the experimenters ; hut may state generally, that, as they were described to us, they resembled those before detailed by correspondents. We could not discover that in any case a table moved towards the north, or any other definite point ; arid we doubt whether a lecture room, occupied by an eager and inquisitive audience, is the best place for attempting to discover the laws nr causes, whatever t hey may be, connected with the much-talkcd-of and tried þÿ table þÿmoving. After each successful experiment, a member of the committee, or the chairman, inquired of each of the
operators whether he or she had abstained from muscular action upon the table ; and in every instance a decided assurance was given in the affirmative.

From the St. Thomas Times, J oli/ 5, 1853. AliAKll OF FIRE. The community was unfortunately again thrown into a temporary state of excitement on Saturday night last, between twelve and one o'clock, by the ringing of the fire hell at Fort Christian, but as there could not be seen any smoke, still less any blaze, many persons were long in leaving their dwellings, and many did not leave them at all until it was ascertained where the fire was, and what was the nature of it. The igniting of a portion of Phosphorus, belonging to the Apothecary llall, and kept in a small wall-room in the next street, and detached from another building, with a cistern of water beneath, caused a smoke to escape through the crevices of the doors, endugh fo be observed from a window of one of tire neighbours, who, on noticing the same, despatched a messenger to the Fort, in order to give the information. Immediately on the Manager of the Apothecary Hall, Mr. 11. II ansen, repairing to the spot, he discovered that the building being so very isolated, and the Phosphorus having no material within its reach to feed on, it might have been left to consume itself in perfect safety. He, nevertheless, immediately caused a cart load or two of sand to be brought to the spot, which he had thrown upon if, and shoveled the whole up and deposited it into some large Italian earthen jars, and on the following day it was conveyed to the sea shore, in the suburbs of the town, where it was thrown, so that any portions which might still be ignited, could consume itself. The precautions

which the previous fire had made it necessary to adopt, proved, in our opinion, adequate to guarantee the impossibility of the Phosphorus þÿ allowing it to ignite þÿ effecting any injury or loss of property. The fear and anxiety which it very naturally, but as afterwards ascertained, very unnecessarily, created in the minds of manv persons, when the first alarm was given, and until the nature and cause of the fire was discovered, appears to us as the only evil now to be regretted.

The launch of the above ship took place yesterday from the Medina Docks, Cowes. The event had been looked forward to for some time by the good folks of the Isle of Wight, i'or the Solent is the largest vessel ever launched into the waters of the Solent, beinrr within three feet of the length of the Great Britain. From an early hour in the morning the people poured into the town, and long before the hour for launching had arrived every shop was closed, all tlie vessels in the harbour were gaily decorated, and one would imagine, from the immense quantity of hunting displayed on shore, that her Majesty's stores had been ransacked for the occasion. The directors of the Royal Mail Company left the pier at Southampton at half-past ten o'clock in the Medina, which had been engaged for the purpose. This splendid little steamer made the passage down the Solent and across to Cowes in 51 minutes against wind and tide. Shortly after the Medina had landed her passengers the shores were knocked away from the Solent, and she glided gently into the water. The launch was one of the most beautiful ever known. The christening ceremony was very gallantlv done by Donna Mannlita, the daughter of the Ex-Governor of Buenos Ayres. Donna Manulita was invited to give the ship her name, out of compliment to the interest taken by her father to establish steam communication with the Rio de la Plata, and we must give credit to the present government of the Republic, for their go al intentions towards the British

company in question. The dimensions of the Solent are as follows : þÿ Beam Length over all 310 feet 3(5 " Depth of hold 28 " Burthen 2,230 tons Nominal power, 400 horses, but capable of working up to (500. The Solent is admitted by the most critical judges of naval architecture to be one of the most beautifully modelled vessels ever turned from the stocks : and great credit is due to Mr. John White, the designer and builder, for his plans and workmanship. The Solent is constructed on the new principle. Her outer scantling is of oak, and horizontal, but, like the Banshee, she has lavs diagonally inside. Below the load line she has four layers, and throughout three; that is, the outer sheathing and two inside transverse diagonal linings of th ce-inch Indian teak. This mode of construction and the use of iron knees throw additional space between decks, and at the same time give strength and lightness. The Solent drew 1) feet forward and 10 feet (5 inches aft, or a mean of 9 feet 9 inches, and as she appeared moored in the river her graceful and elegant appearance was that of a fine clipper, and drew down the admiration of the thousands who witnessed the launch. In a few days the Solent will be towed up to the Thames to receive her engines by Messrs. Miller and Ravenhill. When ready for sea she will make one trip to the West Indies, and then be placed as a regular packet between St. Thomas and Chagres. After the launch the Messrs. White threw open their house to the ladies and
gentlemen, a most distinguished company, invited to see the sight ; and 31 persons sat down to a most sumptuous dejeune.

The Royal Mail Company will shortly have another vessel launched at Northtleet, and on the Tyne a new ship is in a forward state. These three, of about the same tonnage, are intended to reinforce the inter-colonial service in the West Indies, and the company will then have a large reserve ot ships. Two will always he kept ready for sea at St. Thomas's or Jamaica. Though reserve ships cannot prevent breaks down, still it will be a satisfaction to the company and the public to know there are vessels ready to supply the place of a lame duck, for it is impossible to ensure a vessel a against a mishap to machinery. to the proof of the attention paid Hut as machinery of the company's vessels, may it he staled that no serious accident has ever occurred to the engines, and none whatever to their boilers, and they have always returned home under steam (shipwrecks or lire excepted). Since the late arrangement of permitting their trans-Atlantic ships to stop at St. Thomas's the detention of passengers is remedied, and they now are carried on rapidly by the colonial branches to their several destinations. As an earnest of what the company has done and is doing, it may he mentioned that the amount of steam power, in work or under construction, is more than double whit is stipulated for under their contract. The Camilla, a new ship, just purchased for at the Rio de la Plata is expected Southampton in a trade, few days. The Atrato, now receiving her engines, is in a forward state, and in a will months the Royal Mail Company few

have altogether" six new and powerful steamers for the trade, in addition to the present licet. It is confidently anticipated that before long the service between Southampton and Chagres, the entrepot (or Panama, will lie performed brought by regularly in IS days. was I. a Plata The last mail landed at Southampton in less than 'JO days Iroin its shipment at Chagres, and the new ships will still further reduce the time on the voyage. Early in 18.74 we are promised the opening of the railway across the Isthmus of Panama. When the railway is completed, an express train may perform the transit from the Cult' of Mexico to the Pacific in two hours; or the whole of the pusscflgcrs by the steamer, the mail, sea could he dispatched from and goods, to sea in 24 hours. Here, then, we have it practical solution ofa disputed nautical question, for whilst savuns and seamen tire arguing which cape ought to be "doubled" on the outward or homeward voyage by sea direct to Australia, this route, via Panama, will give both the "Horn" and " lloe" the double by steering clear of their tempestuous heads. From what has been here stated, it is evident the Royal Mail Company are buckling on their armour to compete with the other lines of steamers to Australia. þÿ London Morning Herald , June II.

A preliminary meeting of gentlemen interested in the welfare of the fugitive slaves in Canada, was held on Tuesday j afternoon, the 7th instant, at Radley s Hotel, 15 ridge street, Blackfriars. The Karl of Shaftesbury presided. There were present Messrs. Robert Forstcr, Spicer. Ilornan Fisher, Rev. William I,. A. Chamcro v/.ow, .1. James, J. Tvier, C. Galloway, and Rev. James Sherman. The Rev. S. It. Ward, delegate from the Anti-Slaverv Society of Canada, made a very interesting statement of the condition of the fugitive slaves who have escaped to Canada. The number escaping every year was not less than three thousand," and is constantly increasing. The majority arrive at various points on a frontier of seven hundred miles, almost destitute of clothing and ot the necessaries of life. The Anti-Slavery Society I of Canada affords them temporary relief until they procure work, which they 1 1 s 1 1 a 1 1 v do within a week, there being no ease on record in which, except in the ease of sickness, relief had to be extended beyond a period of six days after t heir arrival. I n consequence, however, of the heavy claims of this nature upon the limited means oi the Anti- Slavery Society of Canada, the committee had delegated Mr. Ward to come to England to raise a fund, the interest ol which might be devoted to this special purpose. The Karl of Shaftesbury expressed bis sympathy with the object of was mission, and a commission Mr. Ward's appointed under his lordship to promote it. It

was determined to hold a public meeting at the Freemason's Tavern, at an early day, to ii fiord Mr. Ward an opportunity of making a public statement as to the condition of the fugitive slave in Canada. The Karl ot Shaftesbury having consented to preside on the occasion, a sub-committee was appointed to make the necessary arrangements. Ix the year IH þÿ , the little wateringi place ot \ , on the western coast of Ireland, was much agitated by a circumstance which occurred there. A nice family had come to pass the summer, and were occupying the only large house which A could then produce. We will call tliein by the name ol Trevor. They were people ol The life, and wealthy. the upper class ol father was an Englishman and a clergyman, and had married a niece of the nobleman whose park wall we had just been admiring. And it was a pleasant sight to see Ins tall, slight figure by the side of his still handsome and graceful wile, anil their two fair and fawn-like girls sketching on the shore, or reading on the clifls, or botanizing in the fields, or climbing the rocks for samphire, or visiting among

j the cottages of the poor to teach, or comfort, or relieve, which they did most bountiful! v, and were greatlj beloved in the þÿplace the free hand heingever popular among the Irish. They were always þÿtogether ever forming one group, like the figures in a piece ot statuary ; anil appeared greatly attached, and drawn to each other as much by affection as by community of taste and habit. an addition But one evening they had to their party, in the person of Henry j Trevor, the only son of the family. He I had his mother's soft, dark eye, and his father's tall, slight form, and in all other

respects seemed perfectly identified with the tastes and habits' of his parents and gentle sisters: a hundred new enjoy incuts seemed to have arrived with his presence. The three young people now lived in the open air. Bathing þÿ and Henry was a splendid swimmer þÿ or boating, and Henry was equally expert at the oar or the tiller; or they would go on walking excursions along the dill's and headlands ; or, mounted on rugged little fiery shelties, they would penetrate into the gorges and ravines, and beside the lakes ot the C moun tains, which towered behind their house, the haunts of the hill-fox, the otter, and the large golden eagle. In the month of June the place was visited by a tre mentions storm ; I remember it well. I was then at Brighton, and the loss of life and of craft among the south of En gland lishermen was lamentable. This tempest came suddenly, and went in like manner, dying off in half an hour, after blowing a hurricane all day, as if exhausted by its own strength. The sea scene at \ was grand in the extreme. The immense long bright bil low s ot the Atlantic, crested with foam and lire, fell one after the other, bursting, like thunder-holts, up the beach; and seeming to shake the shore and rocks with the explosions of their dread artillery; or, raging round the worn bases of the cliffs, whose blue heads looked placidly out on the warring waters, like a great mind unshaken amidst t roubles. \t evening a small brig was seen by the red glare of the setting sun, drifting

rapidly on a sunk ledge of rock which guarded the little hay. (At the ebb ot tide a rapid current set northward just outside tliis dangerous reef, hut the tide was flowing now). She evidently was not aware ol the hidden danger till she had struck, and then appeared immovably wedged into the rock. She was seen to hoist signals of distress, and the roar of a solitary gun came shoreward on the wind. Mr. Trevor and his son were watching her from the beach along with many others, and the former now offered a handsome gratuity to those who would launch and man a boat, and go off to her assistance ; hut all shook their heads, for, truth to say, the marine of A was in a very discreditable condition : and, except one middling sized pinnace, they had no craft fit for such a sea as was then running and rag ing before tlieni. On this, Henry Tre vor, leaping into the pinnace, which was rocking in a little cove, protected by a broad, tlat stone from the sea, declared lie would go alone, when four young fellows, who often had rowed him in his fishing expeditions, started forward to share his enterprise and his danger; "it was hut half a mile to the reef" þÿ " the wind was lulling the tide at the full þÿ þÿ and they would go for the love they had for the young master." The cheek of Mr. Trevor waxed deadly pale, but he was a brave and noble-hearted man, and thought his son was in the path of duty; he was a pious man, too, arid felt that God would surely not forsake him. 'I'lie boat was shoved into the surl

amidst the cheers of the men, and the prayers and tears of the women ; and, though every ten seconds it appeared sunk and lost in the trough ol the wave, yet it would mount the next watery bill, and was fast reaching the reef under the long, steady stroke of the practiced liar dy oarsmen. Henry's form was seen in the fast receding light, sitting erect in the stern sheets, and steering with cool ness and skill ; a little gray cloth cap was pulled tightly down over his small and classical head, and the ends of his long black silk-handkerchief blew back in the gale from his fine throat.

n a short time they appeared to have reached the reef and boarded the brig, the strong little pinnace riding under the shelter of her lee. It had been comparatively calm for a brief space, but in a moment a black squall which had been gathering at sea, came rushing and roaring toward the shore, covering the sky and producing instantaneous night ; a mountain-wave swept the vessel, in a moment or two a second, and a third succeeded, till the ship, gradually weakened by these reiterated shocks, entirely broke up, and became a total wreck. Hut where was her crew? They were all saved. In the pale moonlight which ! succeeded the sudden passingaway of the gale, the hardy pinnace might be seen riding amidst the long furrows of the sea, and drifting rapidly in to the shore. Tossed, broken, half-engulfed, and nearlast wave she ever floated on high on ly full of water, she was hurled by the | always the beach, and her crew drenched, stunned, and bruised, yet all preserved from a watery grave. The four young fishermen were there, too, hut one was missing þÿ Edward Trevor was not among the number , and was not found. He had been last seen on the brig's deck assisting a mother and her child into the pinnace, then the "big wave" had broken over them, drenching and stunning all, and they had hastily "cast off" and set to work to "bale the boat, supposing they had the young master on board, but seeing nothing owing to the darkness and confusion, and the difficulty of keeping the boat at all afloat, so crowded and in

such a sea." The agony of Mr. Trevor at this discovery knew no bounds. The unfortunate father would have rushed into the sea to seek his lost son, had he not been prevented by the woman whose life llenry had saved. What was now to be done ? The pinnace could not go back þÿ her keel was broken, and her gunwale stove in ; nor was there any boat to be found which could live in such a sea. All the night long the distracted parents and sisters, hand locked in hand, paced the sands, looking, and watching, and listening, and peering into the darkness; but there was neither voice nor sound, and Henry came not. At a little after two o'clock, the dawn beginning to show, and the sea much calmed, three boats, in one of which was the father, proceeded to the reef, which now stood up in gray and rugged outfine above the ebb of tide. Here not a vestige of the wreck appeared, and, alas! no trace of the brave and beloved one who had periled his young life, and thrown it away in the cause of humanity. All day long the boats continued their search on the reef, and along the neighboring shore. The highest rewards were offered þÿ grappling-irons were used for the discovery of the poor boy, but he was not to be found. At evening his

alas ! its identity could not be doubted, for, in a small side-pocket was Mrs. Trevor's portrait, set in blue enamel and pearl, all marred by the action of the sea-water, a gilt from his mother 011 his going to college some years ago, but nothing more of his came to the shore. Days and days passed on, and every thing that wealth, and influence, and restless, anxious energy could effect, was put in practice, but Henry's loved remains were nowhere found. All language were faint to portray the black shadow which now settled down in terrible darkness over the Trevors. The loud weeping of the gentle girls, the hysterical passion of their mother, continuing for hours, and breaking the health and the heart. The dry, sleepless agony of the father, ever accusing himself as the cause of his son's death,

© UN U & <D 21 44n s and pacing up and down the room in silent misery ; for þÿ ' The grief which does not speak, Whispers the o'er-wrought heart, and bids it break." Their affliction drew them more than ever together. If they were one in the day of joy, how much more in the night of sorrow. Their piety, too, deepened under the trial ; and often, when unable to master their cruel agony, they would fling themselves on their knees, and pour out the overflowings of their distracted spirits in prayer to their heavenly Father; and comfort came down for the time, though hope was dead. Weeks passed on, but the work of j years had wrought on their appearance. Mr. Trevor's once shining black hair was all streaked with gray þÿ silver lines which grief's pale finger had drawn there. His wife's health, like her poor boy's life, was wrecked away. She was unwell þÿ a martyr to shattered nerves. While the fair girls were like | two young trees bentand drooping from the shock of a terrible tempest. They now determined to leave A , the scene of their misery. Their carriage and servants arrived next day, along with an old spaniel, which had belonged to Henry. The sight of this dog aflected the grief-stricken family greatly. Their luggage was all packed, and their carriage ordered to be at the door at day-break, for they had a long day's journey to go. Late in the evening I lie sisters walked on the beach. The sea was calm and beautiful, and the sun dying over it in thin cloudlets of black and gold. They went to the flat

rock, from whence Henry had leaped into the pinnace. They did not speak one word, but, weeping abundantly, each bent down her face to kiss the spot on the rock which their brother's steps had last pressed. The poor girls mingled their tears with the remorseless brine, which now gently came in to caress their feet, as if sorrowing and plaining for its fault. Silently they returned home, and now they all sat together in their little drawing-room. It was their last evening at A , the scene of such happiness, and such misery. It was the hour of family prayer, and Mr. Trevor read that divine chapter, the 14th of John's Gospel, which has brought comfort to thousands of mourners þÿ "Let not your heart be troubled;" sweet words, yet sad. His deep, melodious voice quivered as he read them, for he thought of his fair son lying in the cold sea. Mrs. Trevor hid her face in the cushions of the sofa, and her daughters bent over and tried to soothe her. They knelt in prayer þÿ it was their little wonted evening worship which he had often shared, and always enjoyed. Perhaps they thought o 'that now, and the remembrance might have calmed their spirit. The old dog had been very nervous blue pea-jacket floated 011 shore, and j for the last few minutes, circling and smelling round the room, and whining at the window. Mr. Trevor threw it up. " I sec a man 011 the gravel walk," he said, "who, I think, is our new postillion. I hope Carlo will not hurt him ;" for the dog had leaped out over the window-sill. The next minute a figure

sprang in over the low sash, and with a loud cry precipitated himself toward the party. It was their lost one, whom God had sent them back. "Mother, mother f þÿ take me to your heart, dearest, dearest, mother ! Beloved father, kiss me ! Fdlen, Susan, I am come again never more to part in this world !" "Oh! the deep, the unutterable joy of that moment ! "Oh, God of heaven ! oil, my merciful Saviour!" exclaimed the transported

father, "It is my son þÿ so wan, so worn; but it is indeed my son þÿ my own son !" All this time the mother could not speak ; her face was on her son's shoulder, locked in his tight embrace, and silently straining him again and again to her heart. At length, disengaging herself, and pushing him toward the two fair girls who stood trembling, and all wild and weeping for joy, she turned her to her husband's faithful bosom, saw on his face the old smile come back, which she thought had gone forever, fell into his extended arms, and, lifting up " her happy voice, þÿexclaimed Oh, our God, we thank thee for thy unspeakable mercy, for this our 'son was dead and is alive ; he was lost, and is found !' " His tale was soon told ; he had been knocked down by the giant wave ; his forehead was cut, and he lay senseless under the bulwarks of the deck; a mast had fallen obliquely over him, but had not touched or hurt him. When consciousness returned, he had just time to throw off his coat to swim, when the brig went to pieces, and the recoil of a wave washed him outside the reef into the rapid current which sets strongly there to the north, and completely off the shore. He said he swam but feebly, only using his feet; for the mast had floated with him, and his hands were locked in the rigging, as they drifted together in the sea. He said the last thing he thought he saw, was the light in his father's house on shore; but his eyes were dim; and the last sound he thought he heard, was a wail of soft music played on his sister's

harp. His head was very much astray, he said, just then, and the music appeared to come floating along the waters, but it was a mere phantasy, though he said it made him smile ; and so lie committed his soul and his life to Him who once trod the waves to stillness ; and then all was a blank, till he awoke faint and feeble in a strange bed, and among strange faces þÿ yet saved, most wonderfully saved. He had been picked up by a Scotch fishing smack (which was returning to the island of Skye) at the first break of light. He was all but exanimate when found, and a fierce j fever set in on his exhausted frame at once : but his kind captors took him to their wild but healthy home, where he was tenderly nursed by their women ; and though delirious for a long time, his youth Anally triumphed, and he was spared for the enjoyment and all the bliss of the present moment. He had written on his recovery twice from Skye, but his letters miscarried, and having had a purse of gold with him, which these honest fishermen never interfered with, he went to Glasgow in a fishing boat, and from thence home, where his presence was hailed as a resurrection indeed, and life from the dead.
